utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, everyone. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-A, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to know whether Mr. Simic is able to hear and to follow the proceedings in a language that he understands. Thank you, Mr. Simic. I will now ask for the appearances starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Peter Kremer appearing for the Prosecution with Steffen Wirth and Barbara Goy. Kim Fischer, our case manager, is also assisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me now turn to the Defence of Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic, Defence counsel for Dr. Simic, and my colleagues will present themselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Peter Murphy, also representing Dr. Simic. And with us today we also have Ms. Tatjana Cmeric, and Mr. Jason Moore, an attorney from Houston, Texas in the United States. Your Honour, they have been -- they were involved with the case at the trial stage and have been assisting on a pro bono basis in the appeal. We thought it would be appropriate for them to be hearing for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We find it equally appropriate for them attend the hearing today. Thank you. The Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear oral arguments of the parties in the appeal lodged by Mr. Simic. I will briefly summarise the grounds of appeal raised before the Appeals Chamber in this case, and I will outline the way we shall proceed today. Mr. Simic has appealed the judgement rendered on the 17th of October, 2003, by Trial Chamber II made up of Judge Mumba, the Presiding Judge, Judge Williams, and Judge Lindholm. In the judgement, the Trial Chamber found Blagoje Simic guilty of persecutions, count 1, a crime against humanity; for acts of unlawful arrest and detention of Muslim and Croat civilians in Bosnia; for acts of cruel and inhumane treatment, including beatings, torture, forced labour, assignment -- forced labour assignments, and confinement under inhumane conditions; and for acts of deportation and forcible transfer. Mr. Simic was sentenced by a majority to a term of 17 years of imprisonment. Let me now move to the object or to the subject of the appeal. Mr. Simic filed his appeal against the trial judgement on the 17th of November, 2003. He was then granted leave to file an amended notice of appeal on the 22nd of September, 2004. Mr. Simic has raised 16 grounds of appeal, and I will now summarise them briefly. Under his first and second grounds of appeal, Mr. Simic contends that the Trial Chamber erred by convicting him for participation in a joint criminal enterprise since this form of responsibility had not been pleaded appropriately. Under his grounds three to seven, Mr. Simic challenges the factual and legal findings of the Trial Chamber regarding the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, the aim of which was the persecution of the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac, his intent to participate in this enterprise, and his contribution to the common criminal purpose. Under his grounds of appeal eight to 12, Mr. Simic has challenged the factual findings of the Trial Chamber related to underlying acts of persecutions. In other words, acts of unlawful arrest and detention, acts of cruel and inhumane treatment including beatings, torture, forced labour, and confinement under inhumane conditions. Under his 13th and 14th grounds of appeal, the appellant alleges errors of law and fact related to the acts of deportation and forcible transfer as a crime against humanity, persecution. Under his 16th ground of appeal, Mr. Simic contends that the Trial Chamber erred by refusing to grant him access to medical records of Witness Steven Todorovic filed under seal in the Todorovic case. Finally, under his 18th ground of appeal, Mr. Simic challenged the prison sentence passed against him. The Appeals Chamber would like to recall that in his appeals brief, Mr. Simic stated that he was withdrawing his 15th and 17th grounds of appeal. The Prosecution has submitted that all grounds of appeal raised by Mr. Simic should be denied. As for the proceedings today, in today's hearing the parties can submit their grounds of appeal in the order they see fit and most appropriate. However, I would like to remind the Prosecution and the Defence of Mr. Simic that we invited them to develop a number of issues in the -- in the Scheduling Order dated 5th of May, 2006, and I'm not going to repeat the contents of this scheduling order. I would now like to recall the standards of review applicable to errors of law or fact raised on appeal. The appeal is not a de novo trial, and the appellant cannot just repeat the arguments already submitted at trial. Under Article 25 of the Statute, the arguments raise the by the appellants should be limited to errors on a question of law invalidating the decision and to errors of fact which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Furthermore, the appellant has to submit specific references with regard to supporting elements to its submissions. The hearing of today will be organised according to the Scheduling Order, 5th of May, 2006. First of all, the Defence will part with its submissions between ten past nine and 10.40, and then we'll have a half-hour break, and the Defence will be in a position to continue its submissions until ten past twelve. Then the Prosecution will submit its response for 45 minutes. After the lunch break, between five to one and 2.30 p.m., the Prosecution will continue its submissions from 2.30 p.m. to a quarter past four. After a 30-minute break, the Defence will have one hour, from a quarter to five to a quarter to 6.00 p.m. in order to reply. Finally, Mr. Simic will be invited to take the floor if he wishes to do so for a short statement that should not exceed 15 minutes. It work extremely useful for the Appeals Chamber if the parties submitted their arguments in a clear, ordered, and concise manner. At any moment the Judges will, if necessary, interrupt the parties to put questions to them, or they might raise issues following each one of the submissions. If there aren't any questions related to the way today's hearing will be organised, I would now like to ask the Defence to make its submissions. [In English] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, distinguished members of the Office of the Prosecutor, we have heeded the remarks of the Appeals Chamber, and we do intend at the hearing today to be very concise. So far as the appellant is concerned, we doubt very much whether we will need the amount of time generously allocated to us by the Appeals Chamber, because it will be our submission that this case really comes down in essence to one or two very important principles which are important not only for justice to be done to this appellant, Dr. Simic, but also for the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in a wider context. As you observed, Mr. President, many of the grounds advanced by Dr. Simic are at least partly factual in nature. We are mindful of the standard of review. Indeed, in our -- the first few paragraphs of our brief we dealt with the law on that subject. And to be candid, we do not think that it is necessary to take up the time of the Appeals Chamber by going into detail as to those grounds. We have presented them in some detail. The Prosecution has also responded in considerable detail with regard to the factual findings and the evidence. And so it will be our intention today to focus exclusively on the issues brought to our attention in the Appeals Chamber's order of the 5th of May, and I hope it will be convenient for the Appeals Chamber if we proceed in exactly the order which has been set out on page 3 of the order of the 5th of May, because it seems to us that that is indeed a logical order and that these grounds do follow one from the other in a logical sequence. And therefore, we will be focusing today on two issues. The first one, broadly stated, being the state of the pleadings, the notice given or not given to the appellant in five successive versions of the indictment, not one of which contained the words "joint criminal enterprise," a pre-trial brief, not one page of which referred to a joint criminal enterprise, and even an opening statement that did not provide notice of a joint criminal enterprise. It will be our position that despite the number of times that the Appeals Chamber has admonished the Prosecution that proper notice must be given to the accused. That was not done in this case until a very late stage of the trial. Now, that contention, it's right to say, is not undisputed. The Prosecution has obviously a different view than we do about that, which they will tell you about when their turn comes, but it is our contention that what happened in this case is nothing less than this: That the first time when the appellant Dr. Simic was made aware that he was facing a charge of joint criminal enterprise as opposed to the charge of aiding and abetting, which he had been led to expect, was when the Prosecution replied to his motion for a verdict of acquittal made under Rule 98 bis at the conclusion of the Prosecution's case. And it was not until closing argument that the Prosecution first used the expression that Dr. Simic had been at the apex of a joint criminal enterprise, a fact which the Trial Chamber then in paragraph 994 of their judgement used as the basis for convicting Dr. Simic and imposing a sentence of 17 years upon him. And it is our position, Your Honour, which I will state with absolute candor, that not only is that state of affairs completely unacceptable in terms of fairness, but that this is actually the worst case that this Appeals Chamber has ever been confronted with in that regard and that the time has come when this Appeals Chamber should, with all due respect, express itself in such forcible terms that this will not happen again. Time after time in a succession of cases, Kvocka, Kupreskic, Krnojelac, Blaskic, Krstic, the Appeals Chamber has criticised the Prosecution for failing to observe the rules, for failing to give adequate notice, and yet we're here again discussing this same issue. And I know I've taken that out of chronological sequence, but the fact is that this is a case that really, compared with the facts of those cases is far worse. And so we will submit at the end of the day that it is appropriate now for the Appeals Chamber not only to take the opportunity to restate the law as you have with respect so many cases in the past, but also to take this opportunity to send a message to the Prosecution that the rules cannot be flouted in the casual manner which they have come to expect. We will have occasion to see in the course of argument today that even the Trial Chamber in this case told the Prosecution that they had failed to exercise the degree of diligence, which was to be expected in giving notice to the accused. It said that at page 155 of the judgement. And yet when confronted with this by our appellate brief, what was their response? At page -- at 2.3, paragraph 2.3 of their response, they said the pleadings are perfectly proper, and that has been their position from first to last. As we will see today, Your Honours, the pleadings in this case were not perfectly proper. They were, in fact, such that the accused had no real notice of the true case against him, but worse than that, was in a sense actively misled into thinking that he was defending against a different case, namely that of aiding and abetting. Your Honours, the first issue that you invited us to deal with in the order of the 5th of May was to explain until what stage of trial proceedings they consider that a defective indictment may be cured in order to put the accused on notice of the concrete charges against him and the facts underpinning them in such a timely manner that he is able to prepare his defence. And I turn now firstly to consider that issue. And as I do so, Your Honour, and I know you have instructed us not to repeat simply what's in our brief and I don't want to do that. But I think it is pertinent to -- to point out to the Trial Chamber exactly what the chronological sequence of events was in this case. I would like Your Honours to see the time frame that we're talking about here and how the events unfolded. At this point I experience, Your Honours, some sense of nervousness, because for the first time being roughly of Your Honours' generation I'm going to confront myself with the marvels of technology in the courtroom and try to give Your Honours a visual presentation of what it is that we are talking about here. If you would bear with me here for one moment. Well, I think I'm going to require the assistance of the technical people, Your Honour. They seem to have disabled my mouse in some way. I'm still not getting it on the court screen. Well -- can we ask one of the technical people to come in? Thank you. I'll pause, Your Honours, so I can get some technical help. It's like any show. It worked in rehearsal, and of course on opening night it doesn't. But what the time line is going to show -- here we are. Help is on the way, I think. I'll do it the old fashioned way, while the technician is trying to help. This is the chronology of events: The original indictment in this case was confirmed as long ago as the 21st of July, 1995, and it subsequently went through a number of amendments, the first one being in August of 1998, and the second be just a short time after that in December 1998. Now, at that stage of the proceedings with the Second Amended Indictment it is common ground between the Prosecution and the Defence, I think there is no dispute at all, that at that point there was no language of any kind in the indictment -- ah, there we are. Thank you very much. Your Honour, I'm very grateful to the technical department, and now you'll be able to see visually something of what we're talking about. On the screen there you'll see as I mentioned the confirmation of the first indictment, and I've -- all this procedural history the Trial Chamber meticulously set out in its judgement. I've shown you the paragraph references there. We had the first amended indictment, as I mentioned, and a Second Amended Indictment both in 1998, and as you see, there is no language there of any kind -- Your Honour has it? Good. It's difficult, Your Honour, I know, in this age of modern marvels. We had two amendments. It's common ground really between the Prosecution and the Defence that at that point there was no language at all in the indictment relating to joint criminal enterprise whether specifically or by any other language such as acting in concert or common purpose or anything of that kind. Moving on, we see that -- and this is an important detail, that in December of 1998, the case at that point was assigned not to the Trial Chamber that finally held the trial but to a Pre-Trial Chamber consisting of Judges May, Bennouna and Robson. I think Judge Vaz was substituted at some point. In May 1999, we had the first of two Pre-Trial Conferences. We now I ask Your Honours to notes in 1999, almost four years after the confirmation of the initial indictment and still no mention is made at that Pre-Trial Conference to give the accused any notice of the true nature of the Prosecution's case. In December of 2000, so now more than five years after confirmation of the initial indictment, a very important event. One of the co-accused Steven Todorovic changes his plea to one of guilty, offers to cooperate with the Prosecution, and indeed eventually testifies as a Prosecution witness at the trial. So I think we can infer with some degree of safety that sometime in that period the Prosecutors had spent some time talking to Mr. Todorovic, interviewing him, and gaining access whatever he knew. So now we have five years of Prosecution investigation plus access to information from one of the accused whom Judge Lindholm, incidentally, in his dissenting opinion, referred to as the principal architect of the events that had taken place in Bosanski Samac. So it might have been expected that now the Prosecution would be in a position finally to say to the Defence, "We now understand, although albeit five years later, we now understand what the case is about. You, Dr. Simic, were at the apex of a joint criminal enterprise, and here is an indictment that reflects those facts and gives you notice of the charges that you are going to face at trial." What actually happens is somewhat different. We've now gone to the next slide. In April of 2001, the Prosecution files its pre-trial brief. Now, with respect to this pre-trial brief, the -- the Trial Chamber made a comment, eventually, at 152 of the judgement, and I would like to read to Your Honours briefly. We actually set this out at paragraph 18 of our brief, but because it's of some importance, I would like to take a moment to read. This is the Trial Chamber's evaluation of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. It says this, and I begin the quote: "The Prosecution in its pre-trial brief did not refer specifically to a joint criminal enterprise or any of its possible scenarios or to any of the material basis upon which it is based. While it does contain some mention of the role of the accused, the information is very general and largely a repetition of what is in the amended indictment. The Prosecution pre-trial brief seemed, rather, to be directed at a discussion of the elements of aiding and abetting." I'm sorry, I'm pausing because Judge Vaz may ... Thank you, Your Honour. I'll continue with my quotation. "The Prosecution pre-trial brief seemed, rather, to be directed at a discussion of the elements of aiding and abetting. The matter was not clarified at the Pre-Trial Conference, neither did the Prosecution refer in its opening statement to any form of joint criminal enterprise." That was the Trial Chamber's evaluation of the pre-trial brief, and on reading it it's difficult to disagree. We then move, Your Honour, to what I suspect may be the most contentious issue with respect to the indictment and one which I approach with a certain degree of diffidence. And this is now on the next slide. On the 24th of April, 2001, the Prosecution made a moment for leave to amend the indictment yet again. Now, in the Prosecution's response brief, they asserted that it was this indictment that finally gave notice to the appellant of what the case against him really was. Now, it did not contain the language "joint criminal enterprise," but it contained language which the Prosecution says is the legal equivalent. It referred to acting in concert, it referred to common purpose once, I think reach. But in saying that, I have to tell Your Honours that as we are here today, I believe I'm right in saying that we really don't know what the content of that third amended indictment was, because if you go to the judicial database and retrieve the third amended indictment, indeed as the Prosecution contend it did contain that language, but if you go to the public website of the Tribunal, you'll find a completely different version of the third amended indictment that does not contain any language of that kind at all and is, in fact, in regard to the issue of joint criminal enterprise, is the same exactly as the Second Amended Indictment, i.e., it doesn't refer to it in any manner. This is a very puzzling circumstance, and I'm not sure that I can shed very much light on it, and I'm not sure that the Prosecution at this remove of time can either, but I have to tell you, Your Honours, that there is something very disquieting about this, because I want to take a moment to read a short passage from the motion filed by the Prosecution which resulted in the decision of the 15th of May to grant leave to amend, and this is what was said: It pointed out that Mr. Todorovic had chained his plea, and so they wanted to amend to remove the charges against Mr. Todorovic. And then paragraph 5 of the motion said this: "The charges against Blagoje Simic," this appellant, "Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric remain the same as those in the Second Amended Indictment." Paragraph 6 said: "In regard to Blagoje Simic, it said that the charge of command responsibility under 7(3) was being withdrawn." And then it concluded with the following statement, and I ask Your Honours to pay particular attention to this in paragraph 8 of the motion: "Since the only changes to the indictment are the dismissal of counts and the 7(3) responsibility of Blagoje Simic, there is no need to resubmit confirmation material to the Confirming Judge." And in the decision granting leave to amend -- now, remember, Your Honours, please, we're still before the Pre-Trial Chamber now, not the four Judges who heard the trial. The order signed by Judge Robinson says: "Considering the proposed amendments to the indictment and the reasons given in support thereof, considering that the amendments relate solely to the dismissal of counts and the deletion of charges of responsibility, grants the motion and accepts the filing of the third amended indictment as corrected." Now, we done not know in what circumstances two versions of the third amended indictment are in circulation. The motion that I've just referred to was signed by an attorney, a lawyer who is no longer with the Office of the Prosecutor, and frankly, Your Honour, it is a bewildering circumstance, but it is also, in my submission, a very serious matter and one that gives rise to enormous disquiet. What was the content of the third amended indictment? It seems perfectly clear from the decision signed by the Pre-Trial Chamber that what they thought was happening was that the only changes were the deletion of charges to reflect the plea of guilty of Mr . Todorovic and to withdraw the command responsibility allegations against this appellant Dr. Simic. And yet in some manner another version of that amended indictment containing language said to support the allegation of joint criminal enterprise found its way to the three -- the three new Judges to whom the case was assigned for trial. And what is particularly serious about this, Your Honours, and I come now to -- to move on to the next slide, and you'll see that towards the right of that slide during trial, three months into trial now, December 2001, leave is granted to amend the indictment again, the 20th of December. It contained, actually, a number of amendments, quite substantive amendments, but the one that we focus on is really concerned again with the language "acting in concert together," and what the Prosecution did -- were allowed to do was to amend the indictment to insert that language in a number of different places in the indictment to make it abundantly clear that was going on. And I will read to the Court if I may only one footnote from that decision, footnote 11 on page 7 of the decision, which says this, and it's an interesting comment: "At the commencement of the present proceedings on 11 September 2001, all four defendants were asked to plead to the third amended indictment in the presence of their counsel. The Chamber noted that the third amended indictment which was filed and approved by the Pre-Trial Chamber is the one on which these proceedings are based." And so the question arises, among many other things, what would the Trial Chamber have done had they known -- whether they did know or not -- what the state of their knowledge is we don't know, but what would the Trial Chamber have done in regard to that motion to amend if they had known that the Pre-Trial Chamber thought it was approving a third amended indictment whose only significant was that it deleted charges against the accused? And let three months into trial, and this now is where I come -- Your Honour, have been patient with me in reciting this chronology, but I hope you understand now why I do it, because when we consider the question what is the latest stage at which the defective indictment can be cured, I invite you to look at what happened in this case. Three months into trial, because of the failure of the Prosecution, and we're now over -- we're now over seven years -- six years, rather, from the confirmation of the first indictment, they've had access to Steven Todorovic and six years, three months into trial we're amending the indictment once again, and now it has "acting in concert," written all over it but still not -- nobody has taken a pen, even at this late stage, and writing the words "joint criminal enterprise" somewhere on that indictment. And that is -- Your Honour, that is why I say these rules that the Appeals Chamber has emphasised so often are not academic in nature. These are the most practical rules, because faced with the task of defending an accused in these complex proceedings that this Tribunal deals with, one of the few things that the Defence has to work with and must work with is a knowledge and understanding of what exactly the case against the accused is. Finally, we see that on -- in May of 2002, another accused, Milan Simic, not to be accused with this appellant, no relation, entered a plea of guilty. His case was separated from the rest of the case. And, Your Honour, one of the ironies, one of the anomalies Your Honours have picked up I'm sure by now, another result of the Prosecution's failure to plead its case properly was this: That during the trial two accused pleaded guilty and were sentenced and on what basis were they sentenced? Not on the basis of being a joint criminal enterprise, because nobody knew at that point that was the Prosecution's case, really. And if you look at the sentencing proceedings, certainly against Steven Todorovic, there is no suggestion that he was part of a joint criminal enterprise, and yet in relation to this appellant, whose only fault was that he maintained his plea of not guilty throughout the trial, by the time the trial ends he is not only in a joint criminal enterprise but he's the apex of it as we can see. And it's not until the Prosecution's response to the 98 bis motion, September 2002, a little over seven years from the confirmation of the original indictment that finally, finally the Prosecution reveals the truth and says, "Well, our case is really one about a joint criminal enterprise," and then during closing argument they finally say that Dr. Simic was the apex of that joint criminal enterprise and language which the Trial Chamber adopts and makes a part of its judgement and uses as the basis for convicting Dr. Simic and also to sentencing him to 17 years' imprisonment. And I'll remind -- we'll come back to this later, but I remind the Appeals Chamber that Dr. Simic was not charged with personally committing any crime. The witness Steven Todorovic who admitted to personally committing a number of horrendous crimes in his capacity as chief of police for the municipality received a sentence of 10 years' imprisonment. So, Your Honours, I have -- I'm sorry, I can't remember at what time we were supposed to take the break. Have I overrun my time. 10.40. No, I haven't. So, Your Honour, we -- I come back, then, to the question that the Appeals Chamber has raised: What is the appropriate time, the appropriate stage at which a defective indictment can be cured? We have we -- do have a submission on that, Your Honours, of a fairly definite nature, and it's based upon the fact that a certain reality -- as Your Honours all know being experienced Judges, particularly at this Tribunal, every case that is tried in this Tribunal is of a very complicated nature, hundreds of witnesses, thousands of documents, and pre-trial preparation involves work behind the scenes. As you know, this is an adversarial form of trial. The Defence is responsible for conducting its own investigation. We have to employ investigators to interview witnesses. We have to go and look for documents. It's an enormous amount of work, and all this work has to be accomplished not on the eve of trial but -- but significantly before trial. It's too late when the trial starts. Your Honours know this. When the trial begins in this building, the Defence day after day has to prepare cross-examination. The Prosecution continually will give us further disclosure which we have to digest, and it all gets caught up in frenetic activity. There is no time at that point to sit back and calmly reflect on the strategy. That has to be done prior to trial, it has to be done significantly prior to trial. The issue of whether we were prejudiced, the Trial Chamber, you will recall, having -- while it criticised the Prosecution for its pleadings, said at the same time that there was really no prejudice to the Defence. I think this is at page 155 of the -- of the judgement. The Prosecution jumps on that bandwagon and says, well, of course there was no prejudice. This is at page -- at paragraphs 249 and continuing of the response brief. They say, well, there was no prejudice because, after all, once Dr. Simic found out what nature of the case was, he could have then had witnesses recalled for further cross-examination, or he could have gone out and found further witnesses of his own, or he could have asked for further time to prepare his Defence. The Prosecution overlooked that we did that, actually. We made a motion for that at the close of the Prosecution's case and were denied further time. But Your Honours are all experienced Judges. You know that argument is naive. It's not simply a matter of, well, let's hurriedly revamp our cross-examination because now it's a joint criminal enterprise instead of aiding and abetting. We can't just suddenly take a different tack with a witness this cross-examination and hope that that is going to be effective. If it's a joint criminal enterprise case, we have to know that before trial so that we can investigate it, prepare a cross-examination on a more thorough basis, bring other witnesses, including many of the alleged participants in the joint criminal enterprise who were never called. And the Defence of Dr. Simic was prejudiced at the most fundamental level at a time when it was far too late for him to do anything about it. So what is the rule that we should adopt? Your Honours, I respectfully submit this, and it would be a workable and practical rule, that the Prosecution at the latest should generally plead the case with precision not later than the pre-trial brief. Not later than the pre-trial brief. In other words, when we look at the indictment and we look at the pre-trial brief together, we should at that point be able to say, all right, we now understand what the case is about. The Trial Chamber did in fact, I think, come to a similar conclusion themselves. They seemed to be saying also that if a combination of the indictment and the pre-trial brief were to give sufficient notice that that would be acceptable, and I think that was the basis upon which they ultimately instructed the Prosecution to amend resulting in the fourth amended indictment and finally a fifth amended indictment. But there were two problems with that. Firstly, based on the passage that I've already read to Your Honours, the Trial Chamber itself found that the Prosecution's pre-trial brief did not in fact contain any information about a joint criminal enterprise and that they had not taken any steps to correct it either at the Pre-Trial Conference or during opening statement. And the second problem was that the -- the indictment was amended far too late. We would say that the only amendment that this Appeals Chamber can really rely upon as stating the case is the fourth amended indictment. The Prosecution's going to tell you, well, the third amended indictment is enough and that was before the trial began. But Your Honours have to ask that question, what was the third amended indictment, and the answer is we don't know. We don't know. Because whatever that indictment said or was intended to say I fear may have vanished with the Prosecution personnel responsible for that motion. And that's our basic position, that the Prosecution should believe its case in accordance with the principles that Your Honours have laid down in numerous other cases. The Krnojelac case that we set out in our brief being a good example of that where Your Honours' Chamber put it if I may say so perfectly, that the Prosecution must do two things. Firstly it must plead the case with precision. It must tell the accused exactly what the case is that he must meet and it must do that at the latest, at the latest by the start of trial. And, Your Honours, as a general principle I don't think that could be improved upon. The only gloss that we offer to that is that if Your Honours lay down that it should be in the pre-trial brief, that then sets a benchmark for knowing at exactly what stage we can expect to know. It would be fair to the Prosecution, because by the time they get to the pre-trial brief, they've had time to reflect upon the true nature of the case. They've had time to conclude their investigation, perhaps. And as far as the Defence is concerned, that's really the stage at which we begin to know what the detail of the case is, when we receive that brief. And we submit, Your Honours, that that would be a practical, workable rule that could be applied. And no doubt the Trial Chamber would retain a discretion, as it always does, in a particular case, to say that even if the Prosecution did not meet that standard and the pre-trial brief is not as clear as it should be, perhaps the Trial Chamber could then direct a further amendment of the indictment or say to the Prosecutor, "Look, you know, we'll have a Pre-Trial Conference. At that point you must make it absolutely clear." As Your Honours know the practice seems to be to have the Pre-Trial Conference immediately before the start of trial, so this could present a difficulty, but there might be -- there might be times when the Trial Chamber looking at the way the case is pleaded says, "We will, we think that overall the Prosecution has done an adequate job, and if you clarify it a little bit more at the Pre-Trial Conference then that will be sufficient." The Trial Chamber of course, must retain some degree of discretion. But it's necessary for Your Honours to adopt a general rule. You have asked us what it is, and that would be our response. Your Honours, may I pause and ask whether the Appeals Chamber has any questions as to that submission or anything that I may have said up to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have one question referring to the question of prejudice. In our Rule 7(1), you can read all the modes of liability. I think you will accept that all these modes were accumulatively included already in the first indictment. Is it true that joint criminal enterprise is nothing else but an interpretation of committing a crime and, therefore, your client was put on notice already by the first indictment? And what is the prejudice? What could the Defence have done had it known beforehand that the case was not committed as foreseen in the Statute but the interpretation as joint criminal enterprise? So I'm still not convinced what is the prejudice to your client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the prejudice is this: That joint criminal enterprise is -- is an entirely different mode of spot with its own particular requirements which have been laid down, as Your Honour knows, in a sequence of cases by this Tribunal starting with the Tadic case analysing joint criminal enterprise in a somewhat complicated way but dividing it into three categories of joint criminal enterprise. And one of the problems that arises when one using the phrase "joint criminal enterprise," as Your Honour knows, that is really a shorthand for a number of different possible factual and legal scenarios. Depending upon which type of criminal enterprise we're talking about, the basis on which the case is put is going to be very different. And so what we have to do on the Defence side when we receive an indictment is -- is to try and identify what the scope of the alleged joint criminal enterprise is. It's very important, Your Honour, not just on the basis of liability but on the basis of what sentence may ultimately be imposed on the accused. If -- in this case, for example, not only was it said eventually that Dr. Simic was a participant in the joint criminal enterprise, but he was said to be the apex of it, a fact that made a huge difference. So what we have to do on the Defence side, Your Honour, is to say well, what is the scope of this joint criminal enterprise? Let me give Your Honour an example that may be pertinent and we put this in our brief, both in the original brief and the reply brief. The -- in this Tribunal, as Your Honour notes -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't know whether. The phrase "joint criminal enterprise" as it applied to the Bosanski Samac case turned out to be rather strange. Your Honour knows that in most of the cases where that has been an issue with Serbian accused, it has all really been a question of the so-called vertical joint criminal enterprise coming down from the leadership of the Republika Srpska in Pale through Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, and so on, filtering down to the local level. And Your Honour knows that -- for example, we have documents such as the famous Variant A, Variant B document. Now, early on in this case it could have been supposed, perhaps, that somebody reasonably looking at this case from the Defence standpoint, let's say that we've been given notice it was a joint criminal enterprise case, we could have said, ah, well, in that case then we must look for evidence that we are being connected to the Pale leadership, that Dr. Simic, for example, was getting instructions from Radovan Karadzic rather like Dr. Stakic may have been, and that was going on. And we would have then gone out, conducted an investigation along those lines thinking that we were defending Dr. Simic for a case of that magnitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to interrupt you. Isn't it true that during the trial this was a highly disputed question, whether there was a link between the Variant A, Variant B, and the concrete conduct of Mr. Simic? And therefore, I put the question to you that the Trial Chamber declined to say that there is a link established between these events in Pale and that it has been separate from these events in Pale, and therefore my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, that's exactly my point. We were faced then the then-Trial Chamber -- then the trial counsel is faced with the reality that the allegation is completely different. And this could have been found out because originally Bosanski Samac was a municipality contained in the Plavsic-Krajisnik indictment. It was deleted from that. And the Prosecution's theory ultimately, as it turned out at the end of the day, was that this was a local conspiracy, what I think we've called a horizontal conspiracy or joint criminal enterprise not involving the leadership outside the municipality at all, which -- which -- but simply all the people on the ground, so to speak, Mr. Todorovic, the paramilitaries, the 7th Tactical Unit, everyone who was accused of committing crimes in the municipality, and then Dr. Simic as the Trial Chamber was fond of saying, the most important and influential man in the town, the municipality, is left at the apex. But, Your Honour, when did we find this out if I may ask rhetorically? We found this out certainly at the time when we get a response to the 98 bis motion. If you want to be charitable to the Prosecution, let's say at the time of the fourth amended indictment, but that's really already three months into trial. Now, Your Honour, from an academic point of view, one can -- one can say, well, there's no prejudice because somehow Defence counsel can then turn round and start conducting this new case, but, Your Honours, that's not how it works in the complex world we live in today. You can't prepare a case going to trial thinking that the case is one thing and then it turns out to be another. Your Honour, it's not realistic, and really -- and, Your Honour, at the end of the day not only is it unrealistic, but it's a matter which the Prosecution could so easily have dealt with, so easily have dealt with. After all those years of investigation, after getting the benefit of Mr. Todorovic's knowledge about what went on, Your Honour, they could so easily have remedied this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, Judge Shahabuddeen also has questions for you. Judge Shahabuddeen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, just to clear my mind, are you or are you not saying that JCE is a kind of mantra and that the Prosecution cannot rely on JCE unless it uses that term in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can -- I would not take that position because the phrase "joint criminal enterprise" is, as perhaps I hinted in response to Judge Schomburg's question, no more than an umbrella phrase for different modes of responsibility, which can take quite a wide variety of forms. And one has to say that it would be perhaps possible to plead an indictment with -- with sufficient particularity without using those exact words as long as the indictment made clear, however, what the elements were that the Prosecution alleged. Now, in this case, as I understand it, it may be that I will be corrected at a later stage, but I think the Prosecution's argument here is not so much that those facts were pleaded, and the Trial Chamber certainly didn't think they'd been pleaded, but that by introducing thinks synonymous language acting in concert or common purpose the Prosecution could cure the defect. Your Honour, I don't for a moment suggest that the defect cannot be cured, nor do I suggest that it is strictly necessary to include those specific words, but what is necessary is for the Defence to be left in no doubt as the substance of the allegations. Your Honour, not even the Trial Chamber thought that that had happened, because they took pains more or less to order the Prosecution to amend the indictment twice during trial to get the language right, and it was only at that point they said in the judgement, "Now when these amendments have been made when we read this together with the Prosecution brief defect as that may have been, we can say that the case has at last been pleaded." Your Honour, that was their position. So I would say in answer to Your Honour's question no, it is not strictly necessary, but clearly adequate language must be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask a follow-up question like this: I am perplexed in mind by a question concerning the degree to which an accused person must be involved in the criminality executed by a group before you can arrive at the conclusion that it is necessary or not necessary to rely on JCE. What I mean is this: Is it necessary, from a Prosecution point of view, to rely on the JCE theory whenever it is sought to make the accused liable for a crime committed by a group of people? Is it not useful to distinguish between two scenarios, one involving JCE in which the accused's will is involved in the will of the group; and two, a case in which you can see the crime is committed entirely because of the will of the accused? In that case uses the group merely so to speak as his instruments. In that second case is he not acting independently to execute his criminal intent mainly making use of the members of the group as the instruments of his actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think with respect that Your Honour is exactly right. It's well established, of course, that there can be formed of co-perpetratorship which are distinguishable from joint criminal enterprise, and that is one reason why it's our submission that you don't necessarily cure the defect by simply using language like "acting in concert," because standing alone, that is ambiguous. And as Your Honour says, there can be different forms of committing. And I do agree with Your Honour, respectfully, that, yes, it is possible for the Prosecution to plead precisely a form of commission of certain offences simply by an individual accused possibly with the cooperation or directing others. The only difficulty with that, Your Honour, is then at some point we get in danger as I believe the Trial Chamber did here, and this is really coming to -- moving to another ground, of confusing individual responsibility with what is in effect a form of command responsibility, because once you start talking in terms of one accused controlling a group or directing a group, then of course you have to ask the question, well, was there a line of command, and would it be more appropriate then to charge the accused in that way? I do think, Your Honour, and Your Honour used the term "mantra," and I think that that is an apt observation. I think it's become perhaps a little too easy today for the Prosecution simply to recite that mantra and hope that that will cover up the absence of precision in defining what it is the accused is actually charged with -- with doing. And I think that was part of the problem here, that even when it was finally revealed that our case was one of joint criminal enterprise, the question that the Trial Chamber faced was what exactly was Dr. Simic's contribution? And as Your Honour knows, the Trial Chamber as a result of that became somewhat confused between individual responsibility under 7(1) and what was effectively a hybrid form almost amounting to 7(3), even though Dr. Simic was not charged with 7(3), and that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my colleague, Mr. Pantelic, would like to add a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So before these few words, Judge Liu would like to ask a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Murphy, I just want to know when exactly did you realise that your client has been prejudiced by the deficient pleadings of the Prosecution? From your submission I understand that if not at the submission of the third amended indictment but at least after the Rule 98 bis response that you should have realised that your client was charged with the participation in a joint criminal enterprise. I just want to know what did you do at that stage to cure that defect? Did you raise this issue to the Trial Chamber, make some objections to the deficient indictment, or change of the strategy, as you put it, or calling some witnesses, or even request for a retrial of this case? Because as an experienced lawyer, you know that you could not hold any objections until the appeal stage. It should have made it immediately at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be a good moment, since Mr. Pantelic was at trial and I was not, it may be a good moment for me to ask Mr. Pantelic since you wish to address, and observations too, answer Your Honour's question because he's probably in a better position than I am to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pantelic, just a brief question first for Mr. Murphy, one last question. Mr. Murphy, I have a question. I want to get some information. You said that after the presentation of the Prosecution case Defence requested for some more time, some additional time before presenting its own case. This request, as you say, was denied, but did that have to do with the fact that the -- did it have to do with the mode of responsibility? Did that have to do with the mode of responsibility that your client was accused for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, let me defer to Mr. Pantelic on that because he was involved at that stage and knows the basis. I can tell Your Honour that the motion was made and I know that it was denied. We did reflect that in our -- in our reply brief, but Mr. Pantelic can perhaps give both Your Honour and Judge Liu more full answers to those questions. It may be more useful than my trying to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Pantelic, you have the floor and I'm sorry you had to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Than you, Mr. President. And in addition to what my learned colleague, friend Professor Murphy said, and in response to the questions raised by Honourable Judge Schomburg, Honourable Judge Shahabuddeen, Honourable Judge Liu, and you, Mr. President, Honourable Judge Guney. I will try to summarise that. The position of the Defence in this case was that this case was looked in its entirety with several elements. In general terms, these elements are the indictment, pre-trial brief, pre-trial conference, opening statement, list of witnesses, and the process of the trial in narrow form with all witnesses and all exhibits. The understanding of the Defence in this particular case was based on the, of course, general words of the indictment and specific language of Prosecution pre-trial brief, paragraph 33, where the theory of Prosecution case was, that they will prove that the accused were directly involved or aided and abetted by, inter alia, offering practice Kale assistance, providing psychological and moral support or encouragement to the perpetrators of the crime. The Prosecution theory was that in Samac several individuals committed the crime of persecution on a larger scale with the material facts as follows, and I will respectfully remind this Chamber about this particular fact: The Prosecution stated that before the war 17.000 of non-Serbs lived in the municipality of Samac, and after the Dayton Peace Accord, own 300 of them left. So their theory of the case, which was precisely explained in the indictment and also in pre-trial brief in paragraph 117, was that my client and the other co-accused with the other individuals perpetrated large scale of persecution. More than 16.000 of non-Serbs were forced by the alleged act of these individuals to leave the municipality. At the end of the day, in our judgement, I believe it's paragraph 33, the Trial Chamber found that -- "The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that in the source of the materials by them," et cetera, et cetera, "do not allow for conclusion to be drawn regarding ethnic cleansing or the forcible displacement of the people or the movements of the people for other reasons during the indictment as pleaded in paragraph 28 of the amended indictment." Our understanding and our work as the Defence during trial was to try to prove the innocence of our clients. The Prosecution case failed in material terms. It failed because theory of 16.000, more than 16.000 non-Serbs, which were allegedly expelled simply doesn't exist. And in response to the issue regarding the concept of various form of 7(1) responsibility, I would like to emphasise the issue. We see here after all these years that the Prosecution office very oftenly -- very often use the concept of joint criminal enterprise. I found it somewhere in the library in one of the books I read in regard to this case that -- well, it's a case in some other jurisdiction, of course, and the author said that the concept of joint criminal enterprise is a darling of Prosecution, because whenever they don't have a possibility to fit certain form of responsibility, they are pleading on the theory of joint criminal enterprise. In addition to that, the undisputable fact in our case is that the Prosecution theory of persecution in Bosanski Samac at the scale I explained was linked with the Variant A and B and top level of the administration of Republika Srpska and they failed in our case thanks to the certain success, work of defence, they failed with this theory also. So what they invented with Trial Chamber, they invented sort of village joint criminal enterprise, Samac with a population of a couple of thousand people. So they said, "No, we don't have overall system of joint criminal enterprise. We have horizontal, local level," which is, with all due respect, Your Honour, here in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is absolutely legally unaccented, unacceptable. Now, with the notice of response to acquit the in accordance with Rule 98, well, at the very beginning the understanding of the Defence was that the -- Dr. Simic was the sort of alleged aider and abettor of the crimes committed by the others in Samac case. That was our understanding in accordance with the language of indictment, in accordance with the language of pre-trial brief, in accordance with the Prosecution's submission at the pre-trial conference and opening statement. So at the moment when Prosecution case was over, out of the blue we found that they rely on JCE concept after their case. I'm asking the question: Being in possession of very detailed statement of one of the co-accused and the star witness of the Prosecution, Mr. Todorovic, because he pleaded guilty in year 2000, and now 2001 when we filed this motion for acquittal, why the Prosecution did not use certain elements of his statement and rephrase the word -- words of the indictment and properly pleaded its theory? And in addition, why the Prosecution did not call as the witnesses high-ranking members of the military unit operating in the region of Samac, which is also in accordance with the finding of Trial Chamber are members of so-called local level joint criminal enterprise. Or why the Prosecution did not find certain material, evidence, or a witness statement from the paramilitary units? Because it is well known that Office of the Prosecutor conducting dozens of parallel cases, I'm sure that among all these cases they could find certain material facts and evidences regarding the theory of its case. And finally, Your Honours, I would like to summarise. The understanding of the Dr. Simic Defence was that we are defending our client in its capacity of aider and abettor of certain group in Samac and also without any particular knowledge of the theory of Prosecution case during its case, because all the witnesses and material facts and exhibits presented by the Prosecution during its case were so-called crime base witnesses. None of these witnesses even directed its case towards the issue of concept of joint criminal enterprise. And I would like to thank you for your attention, Your Honours, and I'm free to respond to any of your additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question from Judge Vaz. Judge Vaz, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like to ask the Defence whether throughout the various amendments of the indictment the list of Prosecution witnesses also changed. Were there changes in the list, and did that cause prejudice to the Defence? I would also like you to specify the following: You are telling us that it's only after the presentation of the Prosecution case that the Prosecutor raised the theory of the joint criminal enterprise. Please tell us in what way, in going from aiding and abetting to joint criminal enterprise, please tell us this disturbed your own defence strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would give you a very precise answer. We did not have any additional list of witnesses or exhibits during the Prosecution case in terms of its potential theory of joint criminal enterprise. So we only got the list of witnesses and exhibits regarding the so-called standard of crime base witnesses, victims. Only one of the co-accused who pleaded guilty, Steven Todorovic, was introduced at the end, almost the end of Prosecution case, and also without any word of possible development of the Prosecution theory regarding the joint criminal enterprise. In response to your question regarding the Defence strategy about the Defence case in light of possible shifting of the case of Prosecution, my answer is very simple. The Defence was not disturbed at all with the position of the Prosecution because it was too late for them to shift the and to change the theory. So we were simply presenting our case in -- at our best ability to defend our client in the sense of our understanding of the case, and we knew very well that in accordance with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and some findings of Appeals Chamber that we shall be here at this stage in appeals proceedings that we shall clarify all these issues. I mean, I would like also to make certain reference to Kupreskic Appeals Chamber decision. Well -- and in addition, what my learned friend, Professor Murphy said, we have to respect certain rules, and we have rules here in order to bring justice and to respect justice. It is absolutely unacceptable knowing that all these years passed and suddenly in last couple months this theory was shifted. So as I said, during Defence case, we tried to defend our client in our understanding in light of the exhibits, in light of the witness statements during Prosecution case, and in light of our strategy of cross-examination of these witnesses during Prosecution case in his capacity as alleged aider and abettor of the crime of persecution, because these words "acting in concert together," included only were limited by the direction of Trial Chamber to count 1, which is persecution. And finally in our further submission we shall come to the issue of mens rea and some other elements that we want to bring to your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Sorry. Judge Schomburg would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. The first question, was it not by the direction of the Trial Chamber but based on the fifth amended indictment that joint criminal enterprise as it reads particularly in paragraph 33 of the indictment, the last sentence that joint criminal enterprise was admitted indeed by the Prosecution in relation to count 1 only. But the more important question for me so the following: Did you ever during trial ever object to the presentation of a fifth amended indictment as you say at the late stage of the proceedings on the basis of being prejudiced by this fifth amended indictment before the beginning of the Defence case? Did you take any steps, for example, to ask for additional time for the preparation of the Defence case or rehearing of witnesses having already been heard during the Prosecution case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pantelic, I see that the time has come for a 30-minute break. Therefore, it might be better for you to respond when we convene again after the break in 30 minutes. We will resume at ten past eleven. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pantelic, you have the floor to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Schomburg. Can you please focus on the substance of the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] The question posed by Honourable Judge Schomburg, I would like to say that the Defence objected to the fourth amended indictment, which was by the end of 2001, in the middle of Prosecution case. It was the beginning of December. And the decision on the Prosecution motion for leave to amend the indictment was issued by -- on December 20, 2001. In paragraph 30 of this decision, the Trial Chamber denied Defence request for adjournment in light of the new elements of -- elements of Prosecution theory of the case. In addition to that, I would like to emphasise that the Prosecution did not after the amendment of fourth -- issuance of fourth amended indictment in December 2001 did not provide any additional or a different list of witnesses or exhibits or proofs for its alleged theory of joint criminal enterprise. So the Defence proceeded on the same line of understanding of Prosecution case until the end of its case, Prosecution case, and finally the Defence designed its defence case in accord wants understanding of the elements and the theory of the Prosecution case up to the end of the trial. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just ask. I asked in relation to the leading instrument of this case, that is the fifth amended indictment, and you answered in relation - correct me if I'm wrong - in relation to the fourth amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, fifth amended indictment was issued on -- on May 30 of 2002, when the other co-accused, Mr. Milan Simic pleaded guilty. So it was simply the deletion of his fame and charges against him. It's just technical matter. But the more important form that we are relying on is -- and the issue is the fourth amended indictment in December 2001. So fifth amended indictment, as you see, dealing only with three co-accused, Mr. Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric. This started in 2001 with four co-accused and the fourth was Milan Simic president of the Executive Board of Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, may I ask you for clarification of one small point. You did say that Defence objected to the fourth amended indictment, but you went on to speak as if the concern of the Defence was with an adjournment. Now, what was the position of the Defence? Did the Defence object to the fourth amended indictment, or did the Defence simply ask for an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence objected officially, and at the same time, due to the new elements of Prosecution case, we asked for adjournment of at least three months, and Trial Chamber denied our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pantelic, there aren't any other questions for you at this time. You now have until ten past twelve to proceed with your submissions. You have the floor, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Your Honours, returning to the order of the 5th of May, the second and third questions are really matters which the Appeals Chamber addressed to the Prosecution, and therefore I will defer any observations on those matters until Mr. Kremer and his colleagues have had the opportunity to -- to deal with those. And I would like to turn, if I may, to the fourth, fifth, and sixth issues, which I think are fairly closely related, where Your Honours raise, firstly, two questions about modes of liability, and then lastly a question relating to sentence. And if I could characterise these questions that you have put to us and try to combine them, and I hope that I will not misrepresent them, the issues that we are asked to deal with are, I think really these: If -- if the Appeals Chamber were to consider this case not on the basis of joint criminal enterprise but on some other basis which does -- which was correctly pleaded in the indictments and the pre-trial brief, what would that mode of liability be? What would be the appropriate mode of liability? And can that supported by the findings of the Trial Chamber? And if it can, lastly, what would be the impact on the sentence that was imposed on Dr. Simic? And I think that I can address these three matters fairly concisely together. In our brief, our appellate brief, Your Honours, we -- we dealt at some length with the Trial Chamber's conclusions about Dr. Simic's liability. This is really now coming in a sense to the fourth ground of appeal as to the basis upon which Dr. Simic was convicted. And without going into detail, because I think we did in our brief in paragraph 42 give Your Honours a complete list, as we see it, of the relevant findings made by the Trial Chamber, and I needn't go through all of those, but we summarise the position in this way: We said that essentially what the Trial Chamber did, and one can see it in all of these findings, was make three overarching findings regarding Dr. Simic from which they then proceeded to identify a form of liability. This is at paragraph 41 of our brief. Firstly, they said, well, Dr. Simic was the highest ranking civilian official in the municipality of Samac. Secondly, that despite being in that high-ranking position, he failed to commit the commission -- to prevent the commission of crimes by others, meaning, I think, Todorovic, the paramilitaries, and so on. But thirdly, at the same time, the Trial Chamber conceded that Dr. Simic had in fact no control effectively over the police, over the military, the paramilitaries, or the other claimed wrong-doers. And when we look at the basis upon which Dr. Simic was convicted, it's almost as though the Trial Chamber has convicted him on the basis of not using the power which they thought he had as a high-ranking civilian politician to prevent crimes committed by others. It was not suggested, of course, that Dr. Simic personally committed any crimes. The allegation, rather, was that he simply stood back and did nothing while crimes were committed by others. Now, in our brief we have argued that although -- although clearly there can be liability for omissions, in a situation where the accused has no power to control either de jure or de facto those who are committing the crimes, it is not enough simply that he did nothing. We have cited, as Your Honours will have seen, at some length the Bagilishema case in which Your Honour Judge Guney, of course, was involved in a dissenting opinion, and the Stakic decision as being relevant authorities for looking at how the liability of a high-ranking civilian should be defined for this purpose. Now, the difference between this case and the Stakic case, for example, is that in Stakic the accused was in fact charged both under 7(1) and 7(3). There was, in fact, a live issue of command responsibility. And indeed in this case, up to a certain point, up to the third amended indictment, Dr. Simic was also charged with command responsibility, but for reasons best known to themselves the Prosecution at that point abandoned that allegation and it was deleted. As I read to Your Honours earlier, that was one of the purposes of making the amendment which became the third amended indictment. It's important to emphasise that Dr. Simic was only charged on the basis of individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute, and yet the findings of the Trial Chamber were really exclusively findings that he failed to prevent the commission of crimes by others, which of course is exactly the -- the definition of command responsibility under Article 7(3). But under Article 7(3), it at least comes with this degree of limitation: That the Prosecution would have to prove the existence of some kind of chain of command. We concede, obviously, that a civilian leader, just as a military leader, can be tried under Article 7(3), but it must be shown that there is a chain of command. In this case, the Prosecution conceded that Dr. Simic actually had no authority to control the -- certainly the military or the paramilitary forces, or even over the chief of police, for that matter, and certainly as a de facto matter Dr. Simic clearly had no power. The Prosecution, in a way, in accusing Dr. Simic of failing to exercise his -- what they claim to have been his considerable influence does not then link that to a legal basis for responsibility. They seem to be making almost a moral argument against him in the sense that, well, he should have done something because he was the highest ranking civilian leader. He didn't do it. He had a responsibility. And yet when we -- we -- when it comes to what it is that Dr. Simic actually should have done, what is it that they suggest? In Article 4 of their response brief, they say, well, he should have controlled, let's say, Steven Todorovic, Honour, the chief of police. Your Honour will recall that Judge Lindholm characterised as the principal architect of the events in Samac, who was convicted of -- of very serious crimes he committed personally and, frankly, a man of very evil tendencies. Was Dr. Simic supposed similarly to walk up to a group of paramilitaries armed to the teeth and say, "I'm the president of the Crisis Staff. Stop committing these crimes"? And finally the Prosecution say, well, if all else failed he could have resigned. And I ask rhetorically, what would have been the purpose of that in terms of protecting or helping the citizens of Samac? But they make it into almost a criminal liability based on his moral failure. And let's assume for the sake of argument that that was a moral failure on the part of Dr. Simic. Let's suppose he should have walked up to these armed paramilitaries and Todorovic, the armed chief of police committing these offences when the record showed he was drunk most of the time, and said, "Stop this." Let's suppose that that represented a moral failure on Dr. Simic's part. Does that translate into criminal liability? Well, now, if -- clearly if an omission can sometimes be a basis for criminal responsibility, but we -- but if we analyse the cases in this Tribunal, including the Aleksovski case which we have referred to in our brief in paragraph 44, we see that the -- the omission can only amount to criminal liability where it is in fact a criminal omission, where it is the equivalent of an act, a criminal act, but simply in a negative sense. It's not enough, it's not enough to say that somebody refrain from taking action and that that becomes then an act or omission for which he is criminally responsible. The only time we do that in the jurisprudence in this Tribunal is under Article 3 -- 7(3). Excuse me. Now, it's understandable in a way that the Trial Chamber was confused about the basis for liability because the Prosecution was confused about the basis for liability. We've been discussing so far in relation to the indictment only the possible prejudice to the Defence, only the disadvantages which can accrue to the Defence through this, but I think it's important not to forget that when the Prosecution fails to articulate its case, it also puts the Trial Chamber in a difficulty, because they then have to ascertain as best they can what the theory of criminal responsibility is. And the Trial Chamber clearly did its best given the materials it had to work with, but they were presented with a picture that -- that even at its height, and whatever the moral responsibility of Dr. Simic may have been, when you look at the legal authorities, Aleksovski, Bagilishema, clearly did not amount to criminal responsibility. Dr. Stakic's case as we demonstrate in our brief was entirely different. It was proved that Dr. Stakic had actively been involved in the commission and planning of other offences in numerous ways. He was described as being right at the centre of the activities concerned. No such allegation was made against Dr. Simic. It was simply that he had failed to -- to act. And that was really all of it. So in answer to Your Honours' number 4, is the appellant's spot pleaded in the fifth amended indictment and if so which one and on what basis, I would have to answer in all candor firstly we would say that we stand by our fourth ground of appeal and we say that even if you take every finding of the Trial Chamber at its highest and you make every assumption in favour of the Prosecution, it did not amount to criminal responsibility under the statute of this Tribunal, and I emphasise that, the statute of this Tribunal. It may be that under other criminal law systems we could fashion a form of responsibility that takes that into account, and it may be that if the Prosecution had maintained its theory of Article 7(3) against Dr. Simic it would have provided an appropriate basis, but that, of course, is academic. And so I wanted to make that point first. Then let me go on to say this: If Your Honours are against me on that and if Your Honours feel that the evidence does support some form of liability -- or responsibility on the part of evidence or responsibility on the part of Dr. Simic, that the just resolution of this case when you take into account both the pleadings and evidence and the degree of notice that was given to the Defence, we can say that we certainly did have notice or would have had notice of a theory of aiding and abetting. And certainly if -- if we had to choose, so to speak, the -- the best of several alternatives, we would say that that would do justice to the case. And of course I don't make that as a concession but simply by way of answering Your Honours' question. But it would seem to me that fairness and justice would at least in the sense that Dr. Simic had a fair unity to knoll the case against him, to challenge that case, to present evidence and so on, there can be no question that he was made fully aware of that kind of responsibility and that it would be an appropriate way of -- of dealing with it if Your Honours feel that criminal responsibility does attach. But we would argue if answer to question five, would such -- would the elements of such mode of liability be fulfilled based on the findings in the trial judgement, we would say no, and -- because we have dealt with that at some length in the brief I will not trouble Your Honours by going through that again. So let me lastly -- well, in response to question 6, what would be the effect of a possible requalification of the mode of liability on the sentence, well, we would submit that clearly it would have an effect. Dr. Simic stands convicted as being the apex of the joint criminal enterprise. If that were not true, clearly the position would be very different. In all candor, Your Honours, we would say, and we're going to make a very specific answer to this question, because this is an unusual case in that we do actually have a benchmark to answer that question because we had a divided Trial Chamber. Judge Lindholm, as Your Honours know, took a very different view of the whole issue of criminal responsibility in this case. Although he did vote to convict Dr. Simic, he was -- I don't think I do him any injustice when I say that Judge Lindholm was somewhat skeptical to say the least about the application of joint criminal enterprise in this case. When one reads paragraph 8, paragraph 9 of his dissenting opinion, I think the Judge made that clear. And His Honour reached the conclusion in those paragraphs that what had happened in this case was that certain political and military events occurred in the municipality, and that without any prior conspiracy or joint criminal enterprise, certain people took advantage of the unstable situation to commit a large number of crimes. He found that Dr. Simic had played a role in that, and he thought that the appropriate sentence, and I'm sure His Honour took into account the relative responsibility of Steven Todorovic and others, he found that the appropriate sentence was seven years. Obviously quite a dramatic difference from the majority of the Trial Chamber. And in all candor, Your Honour, we would say that if the Appeals Chamber is minded to requalify the mode of criminal liability in Dr. Simic as we would certainly invite you to consider, we would say in all candor that Judge Lindholm probably got it about right on the issue of sentence. Your Honours, there is only one other matter that I think, having now answered to the best of my ability these questions, there is only one other matter that I would like to address very briefly, and I then will hopefully be able to yield back some of my time subject to any questions that Your Honours may have. Well, perhaps I should pause. Maybe -- perhaps Your Honours have some questions arising from the submissions I've just made on questions 4 to 6. It might be convenient for me to answer at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy, thank you very much for your helpful submissions. I would like your assistance on one point. You were discoursing most engagingly, if I may say so, on the question of omissions, precisely the circumstances in which an omission could grant criminal responsibility, and I think you said the only time that we do that in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is under Article 7, paragraph (3). Are you strong on that, Mr. Murphy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I -- if I put it in that way, let me go back and revise. What I meant to say there was clearly on the basis of the kind of findings that were made in this case, in other words, that when there is no other legal basis for responsibility, the -- we only impose that liability where there is a chain of command and we have -- we have to imply a failure to act. I don't mean to say that omissions can never be a ground of 7(1) responsibility. Indeed, I referred Your Honour to the Aleksovski case where it was made clear that that can be true, but of course it has to be with the same mens rea and other attributes as if it were a positive act, and what we submit is that the Prosecution failed to show that Dr. Simic engaged in that kind of official with -- with the mens rea necessary for criminal responsibility under 7(1). So from that we concluded that the only way to hold him criminally responsible in -- given the findings of the Trial Chamber, would have been under a 7(3) theory which the Prosecution had abandoned. So if I misspoke, Your Honour, that's what I meant to convey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy. I'm grateful to you for those explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, can I think that you have finished with your submission in are you done with your submission?
