utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I have one more matter to address very briefly and that is it is not directly one of the matters that is in the order of the 5th of May, but I think it might be helpful just to comment on it very briefly, and that is our ground of appeal number 3, where we raise what has been known sometimes in the Tribunal as the Celebici rule on circumstantial evidence. This is raised in our brief at page 28. And I can summarise it very briefly by saying that in the Celebici case, the Delalic and others case, the -- page 458 -- paragraph 458 of the Appeals Chamber's judgement, it was -- the Appeals Chamber adopted a rule that in a case that depends on circumstantial evidence, if there was a reasonable explanation consistent with innocence which can be found based upon the of the evidence, a Trial Chamber should adopt that explanation in favour of the accused rather than the -- an explanation that is consistent with guilt. The Prosecution, as I understand it, does not dispute that that is the law. In their brief they, I think, concede that at paragraph 1.4, but in fairness they then do go on to say that the Appeals Chamber should now reconsider that rule. And they cite to the -- in the same paragraphs of their response brief, two decisions one from the United States, one from the House of Lords in England cases which they say have changed that rule about circumstantial evidence. I would like to draw Your Honours' attention specifically to our response to that in the reply brief at paragraphs 2 through 9, because what these cases show when we look at them in detail, and we supplied the Appeals Chamber with the House of Lords' case, it was not given by the Prosecution, but when you look at that decision, what it actually concerns is the appropriate direction to be given to a jury in the common law system of jury trial, and it does not in fact abrogate the rule. It simply says there is no need when dealing with a jury to give them any special direction stemming from the fact that the case is based on circumstantial evidence. Well, clearly in this Tribunal that's not a consideration that really applies, and when you look at the cases involved, Your Honours will see that in fact the rule is alive and well, and from a logical point of view is simply another way of expressing the basic burden and standard of proof, which I think is not in dispute, namely that the Prosecution must prove the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. This is simply another way of saying that. Now, the importance of that, Your Honours, is that the case against Dr. Simic really was a circumstantial case, particularly when one considers the question of mens rea. And as such, the Trial Chamber should have asked itself the question, and indeed really did ask the question, because the Trial Chamber conceded at paragraph 987 of the, they agreed that it was a circumstantial case, and they expressed themselves to be following the Celebici rule. They were conscious of that. And in the judgement, they said, "Yes, we acknowledge that rule, and we will follow it." I trial we submit is that although the Trial Chamber was right to acknowledge the rule, they didn't really follow it because the evidence clearly did show that there was an entirely reasonable explanation for events consistent with the accused's innocence, and I think that really follows certainly as far as any element of joint criminal enterprise is concerned, it follows from the judgement of Judge Lindholm, who provided such an explanation by saying there was a political situation that happened in Samac. People reacted to that situation badly, but there was no preconceived plan. And Judge Lindholm provided a more than reasonable basis for the Trial Chamber to apply the Celebici rule. And if that rule had been properly followed, again I submit that we come to exactly the same result that perhaps Dr. Simic, consistently with that rule, could have been convicted under some other mode of liability but certainly not as a part of a joint criminal enterprise. So I think it would be also helpful to -- to factor that into my submissions on the mode of liability. Your Honour, I will not take the time of the Appeals Chamber by belabouring other matters that we fully addressed in our brief, so if there are no other questions at this time, I will yield the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just to exchange notes with you, as it were, Mr. Murphy, and to make sure that I'm understanding you, your position, as I sum it up if my mind on the Celebici rule is this: That the proposition that the evidence may be consistent with an explanation of innocence, that proposition is not really an independent or additional rule. It's merely an explanation in certain circumstances of what the Prosecution's burden to profits case beyond reasonable doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The House of Lords in the McGreevy case did put it that way, because they said if there was in fact an explanation that was reasonable, that was consistent with innocence, then it could not be said that the Prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: McGreevy's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the McGreevy's case. We have attached the full judgement case to our reply brief if Your Honour would care to look at it. We say that, really, the two things are just logically inseparable, the one really goes with the other. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy, and thank you for being so concise. Now we can give the floor to the Prosecution. We're a bit early. Mr. Kremer, you have the floor, and you can proceed with your submission until five to one. You have 45 minutes for your submission. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just by way of proceeding once we have the lectern, I can inform the Chamber that Mr. Wirth will commence our submissions and will response to the indictment issues and answer questions 1 through 3 inclusive in the Scheduling Order. Ms. Goy and I will respond to questions 4 through 6. Ms. Goy will deal with the moral failure to act or omission argument that Mr. Murphy introduced after the break, and I will deal with the aiding and abetting grounds and the sentencing at the end of our submissions. I don't believe that we will use the full time allotted and we will try to be as concise and precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kremer. Mr. Wirth, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Good morning. I will address you on the matter of pleading the common purpose or joint criminal enterprise doctrine. As Mr. Kremer just announced, I will deal with the first three of the questions that you posed to us and to the Defence. Before I go into the details, I summarise our answers to these questions. The answer to the first question is that an effective indictment can be cured at any point during trial as long as it does not prejudice the ability of the accused to defend himself. If there is late notice but accused informs the Trial Chamber of the impending prejudice and the Trial Chamber provides an adjournment then the late notice can still be timely in the sense that it does not prejudice the Defence. The second question was how the following two positions can be reconciled. One, first position: First position is that the Prosecution's view that the third amended indictment pled all material elements, and the second position, that the Trial Chamber found that the subsequent amendments to the third amended indictment merely harmonised the indictment's language. The short answer is that those two positions can be reconciled because the third amended indictment was admitted in May 2001 and the fourth amended indictment which basically harmonised the third amended indictment was issued subsequently in December 2001. The short answer to the third question is that the term acting in concert together in combination with the term common purpose are classical JCE language. Both terms are contained in the third amended indictment of May 2001. This document notified Simic that he was charged with common purpose or JCE liability. I will now address these three questions in detail starting with the second question since there is potential for misunderstanding. I then turn to the third question, the question of notice, and this will be the main part of my submissions. And then I will answer the first question regarding the curing of indictments. I will close with a short submission on waiver. During my submissions, I will refer to a power point presentation. It's a time line and the Defence received a time line a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Just for the record, I don't get the French translation. I understood, but I don't get the French translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: I will start with the Trial Chamber's second question, and I will try to clarify the relationship of two documents of great importance in the present case, namely the Trial Chamber's decision on the third amended indictment and its decision on the fourth amended indictment. You should now be able to see the relevant filings on the time line on your screens. It appears that the picture is very fuzzy. I don't know if anything can be done about that. All right. Thank you. Now, as I said, the two relevant filings are on your screen. Your question asks how the following two views are reconcilable: The Prosecution's position that the third amended indictment, the third amended indictment, pleads all material elements required for charging joint criminal enterprise and, on the other hand, the finding of the Trial Chamber that amendments to the third amended indictment resulting in the fourth amended indictment amounted merely to harmonising the language of the indictment. The time line on your screen illustrates that leave to file the third amended indictment was granted on 15 May 2001 about four months before the beginning of trial. Leave to file the fourth amended indictment was granted in December 2001 after the commencement of trial. It is important for the present case, as the Trial Chamber correctly stated in paragraph 154 that the words "acting in concert together" were added in the third amended indictment. They were added in May 2001. Now, the most relevant aspect of the subsequent December 2001 decision was that it allowed the Prosecution to insert the phrase "acting in concert together" that was already contained in paragraph 13 of the third amended indictment into such other paragraphs the indictment which already incorporate rated the phrase by reference to paragraph 13. Since the relevant amendment in December 2001 only amounted to explicitly excluding -- excuse me, to explicitly including acting in concert in places where it had already been stated, the Trial Chamber stated that the granted amendments in the fourth amended indictment amounted nothing more than a harmonising the language of the third amended indictment. On this basis, the position that the third amended indictment pled all material elements and that the subsequent amendment merely harmonised the language of the third amended indictment are reconciled. Finally, since the fourth amended indictment only harmonised the language of the third amended indictment, for instance. I now turn to Your Honours' third question on how the words "acting in concert together" notified Simic that he was charged with common purpose or joint criminal enterprise JCE I will address this question as to our broader argument surrounding notice. Simic has raised one simple issue. He claims that the Prosecution should have used the words joint criminal enterprise. His in paragraph 10 of his reply is, and I quote: "The Prosecution did not at any time use the words joint criminal enterprise in any version of the indictment," and this complaint has been repeated during hearing. Simic appears to claim in his written submissions that the only term that could have notified him of common purpose or JCE liability was the term "joint criminal enterprise". In today's submissions, that position was qualified a little bit, and indeed it is the Prosecution's position set out in paragraphs 2.7 to 2.9 of the Prosecution response that the concept of common purpose or JCE liability can also be expressed through other terms including the terms common purpose and acting in con territory together both terms are contained in the third amended indictment and either term would have been sufficient to notify Simic of the charges against him. Taken together, both terms leave no doubt. With the help of a time line I will sets out first that Simic had notice he was charged with common purpose or JCE liability and that it is clear from Simic's conduct during the proceedings that he knew he was charged with common purpose or JCE liability. If you'd just bear with me for a second. Thank you. I turn the third amendment indictment. With regard to this filing I'll first address the terms "common purpose" and "acting in concert together," and then I will address a couple of Simic's additional arguments regarding the second indictment. The third amended indictment in paragraph 40 charged Simic with committing, et cetera, a campaign of persecutions for the common purpose of ridding the Bosanski Samac and Odzak municipalities of all non-Serbs. This common purpose language can be called classical JCE language. It was used in several decisions before and after the Simic proceedings. First, the Tadic Appeal Chamber itself in paragraphs 193, 195, 222, and 229 used the term common purpose interchangeably with the term joint criminal enterprise. Second, a decision of the Trial Chamber in Brdjanin on further amended indictment on June 26, 2001 in paragraph 24 expressly stated that the term common purpose is synonymous with JCE. And the same was repeated by the Appeals Chamber in the jurisdiction decision in Ojdanic of 21 May 2003 in paragraphs 35 and 36. The Chamber stated that the term joint criminal enterprise is preferred, but it refers to the same form of liability as that known as the common purpose doctrine or liability. It is clear from this jurisprudence and from the jurisprudence further referred to in footnote 26 of our response that the term common purpose in the third amended indictment alone is sufficient to clarify that Simic was charged with common purpose or JCE liability. However, the third amended indictment not only uses the term "common purpose," it uses also the term "acting in concert together". As set out in paragraph -- excuse me. Like the term "common purpose" the term "acting in concert together" has been used synonymously with the term joint criminal enterprise. As set out in paragraph 2.8 of the Prosecution response brief, the Krnojelac trial judgement in paragraph 84 held and I quote "The Trial Chamber interprets the words in concert with to connote acting pursuant to a basic joint criminal enterprise." In paragraph 17 of his reply Simic attempts to distinguish Krnojelac. Simic argues that the term acting in concert used in one count of Krnojelac was only understood as joint criminal enterprise because the term joint criminal enterprise was used in another count of the same indictment. This attempt to distinguish -- to distinguish Krnojelac must fail because the same logic would apply in the present case. The term "acting in concert together" must be understood as indicating common purpose liability because the term common purpose is used in the same indictment and not even in a different count. In sum, the third amended indictment using the terms common purpose and acting in concert together used language commonly received in the Tribunal's jurisprudence to denote common purpose or JCE liability. I now turn to a number of additional claims of Simic with regard to the third amended indictment. First, Simic claims that until the Prosecution's 98 bis response of 27 September 2002, which for the first time used the words joint criminal enterprise, he claims that until this time he believed that he charged with aiding and abetting only. This is not convincing. First, the term acting in concert together -- the terms acting in concert together and common purpose cannot understood as limiting the indictment to aiding and abetting. Acting in concert together and common purpose is not language anywhere in our jurisprudence used for aiding and abetting. It is language only used for common purpose or JCE charges. Second, Simic's claim as to what he thought he was charged with is a little bit of a moving target. He now claims that he believed that he was charged with aiding and abetting. At the time, however, in his Rule 98 bis response in 2002, he claimed something different family that the charges against him were overly broad and the Prosecution addressed this shifting position in the Prosecution response brief in paragraph 2.53. A claim from Simic regards the form of the third amended indictment in paragraph 15 of his reply. P the basis for Simic's claim as has been out by my colleague is that the Prosecution when submitting the third amended indictment to the Trial Chamber did not inform the Trial Chamber that the words acting in concert together and common purpose had been inserted into the indictment. Rather, the Prosecution incorrectly stated that the only changes to the indictment were the dismissal of counts and the dismissal of the 7(3) liability of the Blagoje Simic. As the Trial Chamber noted in paragraph 151 of the judgement, it granted leave to file the third amended indictment on the basis that the amendments relate solely to the dismissal of counts and the deletion of charges. It is on this basis that Simic claims that the form of the third amended indictment must be regarded in doubt and that the third amended indictment should somehow not be considered. The Prosecution opposing this submission. The Prosecution opposing this submission for three reasons. First, whether or not the form of the third amended indictment was in doubt, the important matter is it still provided notice of its contents, and Simic does not claim otherwise. Second, Simic had ample opportunity to challenge the formal defect that he perceives to be present in the third amended indictment. However, during trial, he did not do so. He cannot now on appeal raise the matter for the first time in a reply brief. Third, Simic does not and cannot submit that the Trial Chamber had it been fully informed should not have granted leave to file the third amended indictment. Indeed, as paragraph 151 of the judgement shows, the Trial Chamber became aware of the circumstances surrounding the admission of the third amended indictment but never considered it necessary to take any action. Your Honours, my colleagues from the Defence raised a question as to which indictment is actually on the record. They pointed out to you that there is a version of the indictment on the Tribunal's website which differs from the third amended indictment in the form upon which the Prosecution relies. Yesterday, we confirmed with Registry that the third amended indictment which includes the terms "acting in concert together" and common purpose is the only version of the third amended indictment on the record in this case. The third amended indictment as recorded by registry has continuous registry page numbers immediately following the motion to amend filed by the Prosecution on 24 April. The last page of the -- the last page of the motion is registry page 6851. The first page of the third amended indictment is registry page 6850. In other words, the indictment the Prosecution is relying upon is the only one on the record. The indictment on the website is not on the record and cannot be in issue in these proceedings. Another matter that has been raised by Simic, inter alia, during the present hearing: He states that he was surprised by a finding and by submissions by the Prosecution that he was at the apex of the joint criminal enterprise. We submit that such a surprise was unwarranted because the indictment charged him with having been the head of the Crisis Staff and the highest-ranking civil official in the municipality. That is in paragraphs 1 and in paragraph 15 of the third amended indictment. Now, that is certainly compatible with the finding and the charge that he was at the apex of the JCE. Finally, a short note on the comments that opposing counsel made on the scope of joint criminal enterprise. It has been the Prosecution's position throughout trial that there was a greater criminal enterprise based on the Variant A and B documents. We took that position in our final trial brief. We never abandoned it, and we had that position before trial. Now, counsel for the Defence also mentioned that the indictment must -- must make clear what elements were pled. In our response brief in paragraph 210, the Prosecution set out the material elements of joint criminal enterprise as pled in the indictment and the Defence in its reply did not take issue with that. They did not address the matter. With regard to the third amended indictment, it is therefore our conclusion that neither Simic's claim that he was charged with aiding and abetting, nor his arguments about the form of the third amended indictment can detract from the fact that the third amended indictment notified him that he was charged with common purpose or JCE liability. I will now turn to subsequent filings and submissions in the Simic trial and in particular also to Simic's lack of reaction to any of them. This confirms that Simic knew he was charged with common purpose or JCE liability. The first of these subsequent filings is the Prosecution response to Defence motion which start the exclusion of evidence regarding acts of Steven Todorovic. In the filing the Prosecution stated that the indictment charged Simic with acting in concert together with all defendants, including Todorovic, and that therefore acts of an official such as Todorovic were directly relevant. Simic did not react in any way to the fact that the filing clearly implied that Simic was responsible for Todorovic's acts on the basis of having acted together with him. The next document that I would like to refer to is the Trial Chamber's decision of 20 December 2001 granting leave to file the fourth amended indictment, a decision we shortly discussed a few minutes ago. In this decision, the Trial Chamber allows the Prosecution to insert the term "acting in concert together" in name of paragraphs in the indictment after scrupulous examination whether such insertion would prejudice the accused. The Trial Chamber decided that the term "acting in concert together" could only be inserted in such paragraphs the indictment in which it had already been included by reference. It denied the insertion in all other counts. The Trial Chamber stated: "For count 1, persecutions, the Trial Chamber notes that paragraph 13 of the third amended indictment includes the words "acting in concert together". As stated above, it further notes that paragraphs 15 to 18 each include the words: "The commission of the crime of persecutions as described in paragraphs 13 and 14 above. "Therefore, to at these new words to paragraphs 15 to 18, as well as paragraph 19," and paragraph 19 is just an is summarising paragraph, "does not amount to adding any new forms of responsibility but amounts to no more than harmonising the language in the various paragraphs under count 1." This decision clarifies at least two things. The term "acting in concert together" charges of one responsibility and the term is important. This is clear from the attention the Trial Chamber paid to avoiding prejudice to the Defence with regard to this term. And again the Defence did not react. Your Honours, with regard to that very filing, there was a question whether the Defence objected to the fourth amended indictment, and indeed there was litigation surrounding the fourth amended indictment. However, that litigation had nothing to do with the terms "acting in concert together". That litigation related to a count of destruction and elements of a count of destruction that were inserted into the fourth amended indictment. I now turn to the Prosecution's 98 bis response. The response was filed on 27 September 2002, and Simic accepts that since the filing of this response he is on notice. According to Simic, on this date, the words "joint criminal enterprise" from that response notified him that he was charged with joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, this was also the date when Simic must have learned that he had sat through the complete Prosecution case without knowing the case against him. It was the date when he must have learned as he claims now on appeal that he had pursued a strategy radically different from the strategy he would have applied had he known he was charged with joint criminal enterprise responsibility. And counsel for the Defence conceded in that hearing that indeed they were aware of all these facts. How did they react? They did nothing. They did not inform the Trial Chamber that they had spent the whole Prosecution case defending against their own allegation, and they did not request that the Prosecution witnesses -- that Prosecution witnesses should be recalled. They did not request any other remedy, and they did not request more time. Now, despite all these grave problems, Simic did nothing and just continued his defence as if nothing had happened for almost nine months. And it is our submission that that is not a plausible scenario. Simic's silence is incompatible with having just learned that he had spent the whole Prosecution case defending again the wrong allegations. His conduct is comparable with an accused who was not concerned by the Prosecution's 98 bis response because he already knew that he was charged with common purpose or JCE liability. Now, if we look at his -- at his final trial brief, what does Simic have to say about prejudice, about spending the whole Prosecution case ignorant of the true case against him? It is this: "The failure to plead a joint criminal enterprise in this case denied Dr. Simic notice and a fair trial." There are no details about the prejudice suffered. There are not even the very general allegations that Simic now makes in his appeal brief. There's nothing about a different focus of cross-examination and the radically different strategy which he would have taken. And even today, even if the appeal, apart from general allegations Simic cannot specify the different questions he would have asked in cross-examination or the way, the concrete way in which his strategy would have differed and Your Honours have asked a few questions to that effect this morning. In sum, Simic cannot point to any prejudice because he has not suffered any. He knew the case against him. I now turn to Your Honours' second question: Until which point in time the indictment can be cured. My colleague just corrects me. It is obviously Your Honours' first question. Until when an indictment can be cured. Now, paragraphs 26 and 27 of the Naletilic and Martinovic appeal judgement and the Blaskic appeal judgement appear to set out the following: First, as a rule of thumb, a defective indictment can be cured through notice until the beginning of the trial, and the jurisprudence has referred to the opening statement. And it appears that in that regard, there is no fundamental disagreement between the Defence and the Prosecution according to the submissions of counsel for the Defence this morning. Second, the general principle for curing of indictments is that the accused must have received timely, clear, and consistent notice and must have been in a reasonable position to understand the charges against him. Consequently, the timeliness of information cannot be determined in the abstract. It depends on the accused's ability to prepare his defence. If the notice is provided late, the Trial Chamber, on request, can still provide an adjournment and thus render the late notice timely in the sense that the accused's ability to defend is not impaired. Since the accused can request an adjournment which can turn late notice into timely notice, silence from the side of the accused regarding an adjournment must be interpreted as a strong indication that the accused did not feel prejudiced. I turn to the last issue, the issue of waiver. The Prosecution argues in its response brief that the Defence waived its right to raise the matter of defective indictment on appeal. The Defence replied in paragraph 20 of its reply that the matter was raised in the Defence final trial brief and thus not waived. The Prosecution upholds its waiver argument. Paragraph 62 of the Kunarac appeal judgement in a comparable case stated the following, I quote: "In the present instance, the appellants raise the question of the existence of an armed conflict in the municipality of Gacko in Kalinovik in the first time in their Defence time trial brief without substantiating their argument thereby depriving the Prosecutor of her ability to fully litigate the issue. The Appeals Chamber finds this to be unacceptable. If as the appellant suggest the issue was of such importance to their case, the appellants should have raised it at an earlier stage thus giving fair notice to the Prosecutor and allowing her to fully and properly litigate the matter." The Kayishema and Ruzindana trial judgement held something similar in paragraph 64. It held where any particular issue of dispute or dissatisfaction have arisen, the Trial Chamber should have been seized of these concerns in the appropriate manner and at the appropriate time. In the present case, the key issue for any claims regarding lack of notice is whether the proceedings were fair and with regard to this key issue the final trial brief only contains the bear assertion that the trial was unfair but nothing to substantiate that assertion. As in the referenced case law, the fact that Simic sat on his claim for almost nine months must result in a waiver of his right to raise the matter now on appeal. Your Honours, that concludes my submissions, and I am happy to answer questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wirth, am I understanding you correctly, is it your appreciation of the position taken by the Defence this morning that the Defence is saying two things, that it objected to the Prosecution placing reliance on the JCE and that it also asks for an adjournment? utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that is our position. The Defence mentioned a request for an adjournment that we had the opportunity to clarify the matter during the break, and the adjournment the Defence had referred to was an adjournment which was filed, I think, in December 2001, long before the Rule 98 bis submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Wirth, are you finished with your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has until five to one to make further submissions. Twenty-five minutes thus. Ms. Goy, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, Mr. Murphy has touched upon his fourth and fifth ground of appeal regarding the modes of liability and as they were applied by the Trial Chamber. Therefore, I will respond to these fourth and fifth ground of appeal before Mr. Kremer will deal with questions 4 through 6. The essence of the appellant's fourth ground of appeal is that he alleged to have been convicted for his omissions, however the facts found by the Trial Chamber do not support the elements for omissions under 7(1). To this, our position is that the appellant proceeds and a misunderstanding of the Trial Chamber as he was convicted on the basis of his active contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. Only in the alternative, we submit, the Trial Chamber can be interpreted as having based the contribution of Simic on acts and omissions. And even in this case, the Trial Chamber did not commit an error of law. The essence of the appellant's fifth ground is based on a factual error, that on the basis of the evidence, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have come to the conclusion that Simic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise. To this, our position is that the Trial Chamber's findings were more than region the basis of the evidence. I will be addressing the fourth and fifth ground together to show that the Trial Chamber in fact based Simic's conviction and act of conduct and that it was more than region the basis of the evidence. After having addressed our primary position, I will then address the -- our alternative position, the interpretation of the Trial Chamber of having based his contribution on the joint criminal enterprise on acts and omissions. As we have set out in our response brief in paragraphs 4.15 through 4.54, the Trial Chamber based Simic's contribution on active conduct. This is evident from the general finding in paragraph 991. If I might take Your Honours to paragraph 991. In the second sentence, the Trial Chamber stated: "The common goal to commit the acts of persecution could not have been achieved without the joint actions of the police, the paramilitaries, the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA and the Crisis Staff." And the Trial Chamber made the finding of Simic's act of contribution in the preparation of the persecutory act in providing the framework for the joint criminal enterprise and it address it had with regard to the underlying acts of persecution, the unlawful arrests and detention, the cruel and inhumane treatment, the forced labour, and the deportation and forcible transfer. Paragraph 991 and 992 contain the general findings about the role of the Crisis Staff and, in particular, the role of Simic as president in the common plan to persecute the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac municipality. Then in paragraph 994 and following, the Trial Chamber addresses in particular the contribution to the specific underlying acts of persecution. So in the general paragraphs 991 and 992, the Trial Chamber found with regard to the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff was responsible for coordinating the administration of the municipality with the civilian police. 991: The Crisis Staff implemented orders throughout its term that supported the persecution of non-Serbs. 991: The decisions and orders of the Crisis Staff provided the social, legal, and political framework in which the other participants of the joint criminal enterprise worked and profited. 992: And thus the Crisis Staff supported the other members of the joint criminal enterprise. 992: With regard to Simic in particular, the Trial Chamber found, and this has already been referred to today, that as president of the Crisis Staff he was at the apex of the joint criminal enterprise. 992. And his role and authority were essential for the implementation of the common plan of persecution. 992. In our brief, we focused on enumerating the acts of Simic individually and as head of the Crisis Staff, and therefore I will focus here on why his role and authority as head of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency were essential in the implementation of the common plan. During my submissions I will point Your Honour to findings of as well as evidence supporting the Trial Chamber's conclusion. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Goy, I would be grateful if you could speak a bit more slowly, because you're speaking too fast for the interpreters. And you should also allows us to make the connections between what you're saying and the ideas in our own minds. So I would be grateful if you could speak a bit more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I will try to speak more slowly. I will not point to the paragraph numbers in the judgement and the exhibit numbers that are already referred to in our response brief. The Crisis Staff and the War Presidency were the highest civilian authority and involved in all aspects of life in Bosanski Samac. Therefore, a campaign of persecution could not have happened without the involvement of the Crisis Staff and Blagoje Simic as the president. His role was essential, especially if viewed in the context that he was involved before, during and after the forcible takeover of the town, which was essential for the common plan to persecute the non-Serbs. Simic discussed the arrival of the paramilitaries in preparation of the takeover on the 12th of April. Simic announced already in a meeting on the 13th of April that if the other ethnic groups would not agree to a petition of the municipality along ethnic lines the Serbs use force. Simic attended the meeting on the 15th in which the Crisis Staff was established in anticipation of the takeover. Simic was present early on the 17th, the day of the takeover, in Crkvina, where the paramilitaries had gathered before the takeover. Simic telephoned Colonel Nikolic in the early morning of the 17th to inform him that the Crisis Staff of the municipality had been established and that with the assistance of the paramilitaries and the police the Crisis Staff had taken the most important facilities in town in order to take over authority. Simic was involved in the assumption and consolidation of power of the Crisis Staff. On the day of the takeover, the 17th of April, 1992, he was formally appointed head of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff and Simic took full control over the municipality in order to persecute the non-Serbs. Still on the 17th, the Crisis Staff ordered the surrender of weapons. That is Exhibit P77, referred to in paragraph 418, according to which all members of paramilitary Ustasha and Muslim formations had to surrender their weapons. And people who would not comply with this order would be disarmed forcefully and remand in custody of the police station. The Trial Chamber found in paragraphs 451 and 454 that the members of the JNA, the paramilitaries, and the police collected weapons in Bosanski Samac predominantly from Muslim and Croat civilians. The amount of control over the municipality is demonstrated, for example, by the order of the public security station, still on the 17th, prohibiting exit and entry without prior written consent of the police, which according to Exhibit P36, referred to in paragraph 474, was based on prior authorisation of the municipal Crisis Staff. On the 19th of April, 1992, the concentration of power in the hands of the Crisis Staff and Simic, as the president, continued. The Crisis Staff issued a decision on the introduction of a state of emergency, according to which all bodies and institutions of Bosanski Samac ceased to operate and the Crisis Staff shall take up their functions. The Trial Chamber therefore correctly found in paragraph 390 that by assuming the position of the municipal assembly, the Crisis Staff had full authority to govern the municipality of Bosanski Samac and was the highest civilian authority. Once the Crisis Staff had seized power and gained full authority, it continued to consolidate its power. This is demonstrated, for instance, by the decision on the 21st of May, 1992, on dissolving the Crisis Staff of the local communes, Exhibit P106, and the appointment of representatives for the municipal Crisis Staff in the local communes, Exhibit P107. The amount of control is also demonstrated in the decision of the Crisis Staff on the same day, the 21st of May, on the general ban to leave the territory, which according to Exhibit P90 was sent to the public security station and the military command which emphasis the cooperation. The involvement of the Crisis Staff and Simic as the president was necessary for the campaign of persecution as the Crisis Staff controlled all aspects of life in Bosanski Samac, because according to the instructions for the work of the municipal Crisis Staff, that is Exhibit P128, the Crisis Staff was responsible for all areas of life and work, which included providing facilities, providing food, providing medical care. All important members, civilian members, of Bosanski Samac were members of the Crisis Staff. According to the instructions for the municipal Crisis Staff I just mentioned, the members included the president, Simic; the deputy president, the commander of the TO, the president for the Executive Committee, the head of the police, Todorovic; the police participating in the arrests, running the detention facilities and being involved in cruel and humane treatment and the other members were members responsible for economy, humanitarian law, medical care, information, and so on. The head of the municipal department for the Secretariat for National Defence, which was responsible for running the and administrating the forced labour programme was also the immediate of the municipal staff. The head of the responsible reported back to the Crisis Staff, such as the Executive Board P12 referred to paragraph 393. The head for the municipal department for national defence provided a report. The head of the sin exchange committee provided reports to the War Presidency. So the Crisis Staff and especially as its head was at the top and coordinating the civilian authorities as can be seen from the instructions of the municipal Crisis Staff. It not only coordinated the civilian authorities but also cooperated with the paramilitaries and the JNA. The connection with the military, which was also involved in arrests, detention, cruel and inhumane treatment is obvious from the same instructions for the municipality according to which the Crisis Staff was obliged to provide working and living conditions for the JNA and thus supported the activities of the JNA. The Crisis Staff ordered the organisation of feeding of soldiers and paramilitaries, ordered the purchase of uniforms, and moreover was in contact and cooperation with the military which is supported by the fact that Simic was in contact with Colonel Nikolic before the takeover and informed him immediately after the takeover as found in paragraphs 384, 989 and 446, 990. Contact and cooperation with the paramilitaries who were involved in the unlawful arrests and detention, cruel and inhumane treatment is demonstrated by the fact that Simic influenced the removal of Colonel Djordjevic and the replacement with Crni and that Simic requested the return of the paramilitaries to Bosanski Samac in October. The cooperation with the military, the paramilitaries, and the police is also confirmed in contemporary documents such as Exhibit P127 as well as Exhibits P115 and P117. When the Crisis Staff became the War Presidency, the regime remained the same, as the Crisis Staff was just renamed. That is Exhibit P73, referred to in paragraph 391. According to Article 3, the War Presidency shall operate in wartime as the highest body of authority in the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, and Simic was the president. The Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, which with Simic as the president set up organs to help to implement the common plan. The War Presidency set up the commission for exchange of prisoners. Simic was involved in the appointment of the head of the municipal department of the Secretariat for National Defence, the body managing the forced labour programme. The Crisis Staff established an executive board to execute its decisions. The executive board was involved in the forced labour programme. The Crisis Staff would also dismiss people in important positions like, for example, a factory director. That is Exhibit P172. And use its influence, for example, in the removal of Colonel Djordjevic in order to have him replaced with Crni. All these findings and evidence support the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Simic's role and authority were essential for the implementation of the common plan in Bosanski Samac. Providing the framework and the support to the other members of the joint criminal enterprise to carry out the underlying acts of persecution would have been sufficient to find him liable for having contributed to the joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber, however, more specifically addressed his contribution with regard to the underlying acts of persecution. Regarding the unlawful arrests and detentions, the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 994, refers to the framework role just discussed by -- by finding that Simic was the highest ranking civilian official. That is the beginning of 994. Simic consolidated Serb institutions and coordinated the functions. Simic presided over meetings where operations of authorities were discussed and in which Todorovic, the chief of police, was report on the situations of arrests and detentions. Simic had strong influence over arrests and detention. That is paragraph 995. And the Trial Chamber correctly concluded, 996, that the police, the paramilitaries, the Crisis Staff, and the JNA worked together to maintain the system of arrests and detention. Similarly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Goy, you have five minutes left before the break at five to one. Please try to conclude your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Similarly regarding cruel and inhumane treatment, the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 1004 that the police, the military, and the paramilitaries were working hand and hand together and steering the municipality. The framework of this to the structure of the municipality with regard to the maintenance of the system of detention is obvious, for example, from the statement of witness Vladimir Sarkanovic referred to in paragraph 604 that the detention facilities in Bosanski Samac could only have been established and maintained by the Serb authorities in control of Bosanski Samac in coordination with Steven Todorovic. The Crisis Staff therefore provided inappropriate detention facilities, inappropriate medical care, and Simic was personally involved in the release of important prisoners because he was contacted, for example, with regard to members of the JNA and Sulejman Tihic who was the local head of the SDA. And thus the Trial Chamber correctly concluded in paragraph 995 that he had strong influence over the arrests and detentions. If I may, I would like to pause here in order to arrest the specific contributions with regard to forced labour and deportation after the break. Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.
