So we have to take that into account. Thank you very much. The hearing stands adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing resumes. [In English] You will have one hour, 30 minutes to submit the rest of.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break, I referred to findings in evidence regarding the role and authority of Dr. Simic in the implementation of the common plan and how this contribution to the framework has been addressed in the context of the underlying acts of arrests and detention and cruel and inhuman treatment. I would now like to address the last two underlying acts, the forced labour and deportation and forcible transfer. Similar to the other underlying acts, the Trial Chamber referred to how the providing of the framework had an impact on the underlying act and addressed the individual acts of Mr. Simic. Regarding forced labour, Simic was involved in participating in the appointment of the head of the municipal department for national defence, the body managing the forced labour programme. They had reported back to the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff was mentioned on call-up papers for work obligations as evident from the testimony of Witness M referred to in paragraph 813. Moreover, requests for workers were channeled through the executive board as evident from Exhibit D 125/1 and the testimony of Bozo Ninkovic referred to in paragraph 812. The Executive Board was set up by the Crisis Staff, as I have referred to earlier. The Crisis Staff gave its general consent to the request of workers and in some occasions the Crisis Staff was directly addressed with requests of workers, so by Savo Popovic, Crisis Staff member regarding repair work in Odzak. That is the evidence of Steven Todorovic in paragraph 825 of the Trial Chamber judgement. The same applied for deportation and forcible transfer. The Crisis Staff -- or, rather, the War Presidency at that stage established the Exchange Commission, and Simic and the Crisis Staff were also involved in deportations and forcible transfer such as with regard to the Serb detainees in Odzak. As the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 1036, Simic was informed of the negotiations by Simo Zaric. The Crisis Staff headed by Simic proposed to participate in the exchange. Involvement is further demonstrated by Exhibit P99, referred to in paragraph 919, a letter dealing with the situation of Serbs in Odzak, as well as Exhibit P82. The Crisis Staff headed by Simic, moreover, ordered Miroslav Tadic, Simo Zaric, and Bozo Ninkovic to compile lists of detainees. To conclude, the Trial Chamber found that Simic in many ways actively contributed to the underlying acts of persecution to the common plan to persecute the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, and on the basis of all the evidence, the Trial Chamber's conclusion was more than reasonable. As regards Simic's inaction, first of all, we submit that by doing nothing to impede the furthering of the common plan, he maintained the system that supported other members of the joint criminal enterprise. Therefore, it demonstrates a positive contribution to the system. Moreover, in our submission, the Trial Chamber referred to omission not as a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise but as evidence for the fact that Simic shared the intent with the other members of the joint criminal enterprise. This is obvious, in our submission, from the structure of the trial judgement. I've pointed out that paragraph 991 and paragraph 992 contain the general findings on the active contribution. Then, for example, with regard to the first underlying act of persecution, the unlawful arrests and detentions, the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 994, first refers to this framework by mentioning that Simic oversaw key objectives. That included consolidated institutions, coordinating functions, presiding over meetings, so refers to the actions I've set out before. Then the trial judgement continues by saying that he did have authority and influence and the obligation to do certain things which he didn't do. The same structure can be found in paragraph 996. The Trial Chamber found in the middle of the paragraph that the police, the paramilitaries, the Crisis Staff, and the JNA worked together to maintain the systems of arrests and detention. Then the Trial Chamber found that Simic did nothing to assist or release the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg has a question. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. So in short, we submit that the structure by first referring to action, then referring to inaction, and concluding in paragraph 997 that the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from these facts is that Simic shared the intent in our submission supports our argument that the omission was used as evidence for the shared intent. And the same structure can be found for the underlying acts of persecution. Therefore, we would conclude that in our primary position the Trial Chamber did not err in law or in fact in basing Simic's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise on active conduct. This finishes my submissions with regard to our primary position, and only in the alternative, we submit, the Trial Chamber can be interpreted as having based the contributions on acts as well as on omissions but only in addition did the Trial Chamber, in addition to the act of conduct I've laid out before, did the Trial Chamber take omission into account. And as I've set out before, the acts of contribution in themselves would have been sufficient to find Simic liable on the basis of joint criminal enterprise and, therefore, where that is error with regard to the omission does not have an impact on the conviction for participation in the joint criminal enterprise. Therefore, I leave did to the Appeals Chamber whether Your Honours would like to hear submissions on omission as a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. I may repeat. In our submission, because even in our alternative argument, the omissions were used only in addition to the act of conduct. Any error with regard to the omission would not have an impact on the conviction for contribution in the joint criminal enterprise. And therefore, we are prepared to make submissions on the question of omission, but we leave it to Your Honours whether you would like us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Okay. We would like to hear you on this point, as long as you don't exceed, you don't go beyond the time limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I will try to be brief, Your Honour. As we have set out in our brief and has been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in the Kvocka appeal in paragraph 187, contribution to the joint criminal enterprise can be based on act of conduct or on omission. And the requirements for that are met in this case. Simic had a duty to ensure protection for the civilian population. The Trial Chamber found that the Crisis Staff had to ensure health, safety, and welfare of the population. And it based it, inter alia, on the instructions for work of the municipal Crisis Staff. The Defence seems to take issue with the fact that the -- a duty can be based in domestic law in order to right an international criminal liability. Domestic law, in our submission, at least determines which individual is the addressee of the duty. This can be found, for example, in the ICRC protocol I Article 86, paragraph 3537 where it commentary says that the national law of the state establishes the powers and the duties of the civilians. And whether it is in general sufficient to rely purely on domestic law in order to find the duty to act does not in our submission need to be decided in this case. The reason is that in the case at hand, Simic had a duty based international law to ensure protection for the civilian population. Rule 87 of the customary international law study of the ICRC says that civilians and persons hors de combat must be treated humanely in armed conflict regardless of the nature of the conflict. That is based on inter alia Common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions and Articles of both additional protocols. A specific subset of the duty is the duty to protection of persons deprived of their liberty as were the majority of the victims in this case. Although the duty is technically incumbent on the state, it has been accepted, for example, in the Blaskic appeal judgement in paragraph 663, that while these duties are technically incumbent on the state, they have resulted in a recognition of a general principle of criminal liability for omission. This international duty to ensure respect of fundamental rights by public officials is confirmed in the context of crimes against humanity by the trial judgement of the ICTR in the case of Rutaganira. And if I may just quote from two paragraphs of that judgement. I will quote in French because there is no English translation available at this time. I will quote from paragraph 78: "[Interpretation] Under international law, any individual vested with public authority has the duty to act to protect human beings." [In English] It concluded in paragraph 79, and I will again quote in French: "[Interpretation] As a result, any public official has the duty not only to respect fundamental human rights as any other individual but also to make sure that these rights are respected." [In English] Simic, in our submission is the addressee of this duty because he was the head of the Crisis Staff, the War Presidency, and the municipal assembly in the municipality. He represented the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg, question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but that we stay in context. Is it your proposition that also a person who allegedly referred to the fifth amended indictment, paragraph 13(A), who is alleged to have forcibly taken over the municipality of Bosanski Samac by Serb forces, therefore illegally taking this position, that such a person has the same obligation under international law? That on the one hand the Prosecutor submits that it was illegal to take over Bosanski Samac, and on other hand, when you have done so illegally, then you have to take these steps foreseen under international law, as you submit, for regular superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: It would be our submission that the duty can arise from factually the duty is incumbent on the fact that they have taken over control of the situation and factually take control of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. So we would submit that the illegal character of the forcible takeover does not undermine the obligation to ensure protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. To conclude, we would submit that will the Trial Chamber correctly found that Simic had to ensure protection for the civilian population and therefore met the criteria for omission as a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, namely that he had the duty to act. He, moreover, as we have set out in our brief, also had the ability to act. We have set out in the brief that although generally liability for commission through omission requires the ability to prevent the crime, in case of a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise by omission, the same has to apply as with regard to active contribution. For active contribution, it just needs to be a contribution, not a substantial contribution or significant contribution as set out by the Appeals Chamber. The contribution does not need to be a "but, for" contribution. And similarly, with regard to omission, it does not need to be the ability to prevent by taking action but just the ability to impede, to make it more difficult for the others if action is taken. And the findings by the Trial Chamber support that Simic had the position to make it more difficult. He, as found by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 994, was in a position of strong influence and control. He could have turned to the Prime Minister of the Republika Srpska. He could have expressed and used his influence and control with regard to the other perpetrators. He could have used his influence to try to release prisoners, to try to take measures with regard to appropriate detention facilities and appropriate medical care. He had the ability to impede the furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise. He did not do that. Therefore, we submit that he failed to comply with his duty. Therefore, even if the Trial Chamber based the contribution on acts and omissions, the fourth and the fifth ground should be dismissed. This ends my submissions, and I'm available for Your Honours' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Judge Liu has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I would like you to enlighten me about the differences between the omission in the joint criminal enterprise and the command responsibility which the Prosecution drew up in their indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: There are essentially two differences. The first one is that an omission in the joint criminal enterprise requires that the participant shares the common purpose, shares the intent with the other members of the joint criminal enterprise. With regards to liability as a superior, it is not required that he shares the intent. Furthermore, with regard to the duty to act, in a 7(3) liability, the duty results from the control over the subordinates. In -- in the contribution to the joint criminal enterprise by omission, it can be the duty like it is in this case, to ensure protection for the victims, which does not necessarily be linked with the control over the physical perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: You want to proceed, Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I will deal with questions 4, 5, and 6 in the Scheduling Order. Under the mode of liability section in the Scheduling Order, the Appeals Chamber asked the parties to comment on what other mode of liability pleaded in the fifth amended indictment best characterises Simic's liability, which one and on what basis. My learned friend, Mr. Murphy, has conceded that aiding and abetting is an appropriate alternative mode of liability and has stated in his remarks that it was appropriately pleaded. In fact, that conclusion is held by the Trial Chamber to be consistent to the evidence. I refer you to paragraph 136 of the Trial Chamber where they state: "Only two heads of responsibility were applicable, JCE and aiding and abetting." Because the Trial Chamber based Mr. Simic's responsibility on joint criminal enterprise, it did not apply its findings using aiding and abetting. If JCE was not properly proceeded in the indictment, then Simic's criminal responsibility can be justified under aiding and abetting. For Simic, aiding and abetting persecution is referred to in the indictment specifically in paragraphs 11, 13, 16, and 33. The Trial Chamber, as my colleague Ms. Goy has just finished referring you to, has ample findings of Simic's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. The elements of aiding and abetting require contribution, and our position will be that the contribution that was found by the Trial Chamber is sufficient to support a finding of contribution of aiding and abetting the perpetrators of the joint criminal enterprise in persecutions of the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac. The elements for aiding and abetting are most recently referred to by this Chamber in the decision of Kvocka at paragraph 89, quoting from Vasiljevic Appeals Chamber judgement. In Kvocka, the Court says for the actus reus, the aider and abettor carries out acts specifically directed to assist, encourage, or lend moral support to the perpetration of certain specific crime, and then in quotations, murder or parenthesis, murder E extermination, rape, torture, wanton destruction of civilian property, et cetera, and we would include the crime persecution, and this support has a substantial effect upon the perpetration of the crime. As to mens rea, in the case of aiding and abetting, in the same paragraph, the requisite element is knowledge that the acts performed bit aider and abettor assists the specific crime of the principal. I note by way of passing in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision that what constitutes knowledge under this heading was discussed and an issue has been raised in the Blagojevic and Jokic appeal in respect of how the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision should be interpreted, but for our purposes it's not necessary to go there because the findings of knowledge by the Trial Chamber are sufficient for the purposes of arguing based on knowledge simpliciter. This Chamber went further in Kvocka to draw a distinction between aider and abettor and a member of a joint criminal enterprise at paragraph 90 where you stated whether aider and abettor is responsible for assisting an individual crime committed by a single perpetrator for assisting in all crimes committed by a plurality of persons involved in a joint criminal enterprise depends on the effect of the assistance and on the knowledge of the accused. The requirement that an aider and abettor make a substantial submission to the crime assisting a crime committed by an individual or in crimes committed by a plurality of persons. Furthermore, the requisite mental element applies equally to an aiding and abetting a crime committed by an individual or a plurality of persons where the aider and abettor only knows that his assistance is helping a single person to commit a crime he is only liable for aiding and abetting that crime. This is so even go the principal perpetrator is part of a joint criminal enterprise involving the commission of further crimes. The Appeals Chamber then goes on in paragraph 91 to emphasise that joint criminal enterprise is simply a means of committing a crime and it is not a crime itself. Therefore, it would be inaccurate to referring to aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise. The aider and abettor assists the principal perpetrator or perpetrators of the crime. Now, Ms. Goy has reviewed extensively the findings of contribution by the Trial Chamber under joint criminal enterprise referred to in the judgement and in the evidence both in terms of the framework evidence and in respect to the individual acts and contributions in respect of the crimes or acts underlying the persecutions. Our position is that the contributions found by the Trial Chamber in its judgement are substantial and establish beyond any doubt that Simic assisted the participants that are listed in the indictment persecute the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac. The participants are listed in paragraph 984 of the Trial Chamber's decision. The participants include the other members of the Crisis Staff, the Serb police including Todorovic, the Serb paramilitaries, and the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, all of whom are mentioned in the indictment. The crime that is assisted by Mr. Simic to persecute the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac by a variety of acts, and the contribution, the contribution of Simic to the participants in committing this crime went beyond assistance, went beyond encouragement, went beyond lending moral support. His contribution was more tangible. Simic knew of the persecutory plan. Simic knew its principals and Simic supported and worked with them as the president of the Crisis Staff and of the War Presidency and the municipal assembly. His support and that of the organs that he was president of was essential to the success and carrying out of the plan to persecute the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac. And the contributions are clearly found in the Trial Chamber Judgement, some of which have been set out by Ms. Goy earlier and others of which are referred to in our written submissions. The determination, should you make it, that the indictment was effective in pleading a joint criminal enterprise, in our respectful submission, would not underline the finding that a joint criminal enterprise existed and that Simic's active contribution supported its participants. Although this finding that the indictment was defective would bar a finding that Simic had criminal responsibility based on his contribution to the JCE, based on fairness grounds solely it cannot prevent a finding of criminal responsibility based on participation by aiding and abetting the members of the JCE in committing persecution. The actus reus of aiding and abetting may occur both before, during, and after the principal crime has been perpetrated. In this particular case, Simic's contribution was before and during the commission of the principle crime of persecution through contributing to the various and many underlying acts that supported it. Ms. Goy has referred you to his contributions before and during and contributing to not only the takeover but also in installing himself as president of the Crisis Staff and involved in establishing and continuing and coordinating the various organs and functions that supported the persecutory conduct of the members of the joint criminal enterprise. Our position in terms of his substantive contribution based solely on the findings of the Trial Chamber showed clearly that Simic by his actions, positively and substantially, aided and abetted the perpetrators of the persecution of the non-Serb population in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. The next question, then, is, did Mr. Simic know that his contributions assisted or facilitated the persecution of non-Serbs by the members of the JCE? Not only did the Trial Chamber find that Simic knew, but it also concluded that Simic shared their intent, at paragraph 997. In terms of knowledge generally, the Trial Chamber, and I'll just be quoting from its various paragraphs on the various points where they talk about knowledge, on the question of knowledge generally, at paragraph 992, the Trial Chamber concluded in the second sentence: "Blagoje Simic knew that his role and authority were essential for the accomplishment of the common goal of persecution." Towards the end of the paragraph, still 992: "The Trial Chamber is convinced that Blagoje Simic and the other participants acted with the shared intent to pursue this goal, the goal being persecution of the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac." Specific knowledge as to the underlying acts is also specifically found by the Trial Chamber. Knowledge about arrests, paragraph 995: "Blagoje Simic was aware of the persecution of non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac municipality. Blagoje Simic was informed of the continued arrests and detention of non-Serbs during the conflict and was in a position to express persuasive opinions and at meetings with principal actors in the joint criminal enterprise." Paragraph 996: "He had to be aware of civilians being detained in facilities that included the SUP, TO, and primary and secondary schools in Bosanski Samac. He was also aware that detainees were held in camps in Zasavica and Crkvina, and transferred from the TO in Brcko and detained in other facilities presided over by the JNA in Bijeljina. The police, the paramilitaries, the Crisis Staff, and JNA worked together to maintain the system of arrests and detention." Knowledge of cruel treatment, cruel and inhumane treatment, paragraph 1008: "Blagoje Simic knew about the cruel and inhumane treatment, including the beatings, the torture, and the inhumane confinement conditions of the non-Serb prisoners in detention facilities in Bosanski Samac." The last sentence: "The Trial Chamber does not accept Blagoje Simic's testimony that he did not know about such mistreatment." Paragraph 1010: "The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the only conclusion that can be drawn from the above-mentioned evidence and from the fact that Blagoje Simic continued to act as the highest ranking civilian during the indictment period is that he shared the discriminatory intent of the other participants in the joint criminal enterprise to persecute the non-Serb population of the municipality of Bosanski Samac through cruel and inhumane treatment including beatings, torture, and confinement under inhumane conditions." Knowledge of forced labour, paragraph 1021: "Blagoje Simic knew that Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were forced to perform dangerous or humiliating work. Blagoje Simic was aware of the existence of the forced labour programme." And finally, with respect to deportation and forcible transfer, paragraph 1036: "With regard to the forcible transfer of Osman Jasarevic on 25, 26 May, 1992, in Dubica, the Trial Chamber finds that Blagoje Simic and other members of the Crisis Staff were informed by Simo Zaric about the negotiations Simo Zaric had had with the Odzak side prior to this exchange. Simo Zaric told the Odzak Exchange Commission that he could put proposals for this exchange to the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff, and after he informed Blagoje Simic about this proposed exchange. Blagoje Simic had nothing against an all-for-all exchange. Blagoje Simic also testified that the Crisis Staff proposed to the Republic Exchange Commission to participated in the exchange." And finally 1037, still dealing with deportations and forcible transfers: "Miroslav Tadic informed the Crisis Staff regularly about the exchanges and that on the 2nd of October, 1992, Blagoje Simic signed P83 as the president of the War Presidency, thereby appointing the civil -- Civilian Exchange Committee that reported on its activities on a monthly basis to the War Presidency." One can only conclude from the findings of the Trial Chamber both as to acts and contribution and in respect to knowledge that aiding and abetting, which was pleaded in the indictment, was proven at trial. Simic's contribution for persecution -- or conviction for persecution can be maintained under aiding and abetting as a mode of liability based on the same findings the Trial Chamber used to convict him as a member of the joint criminal enterprise. If the Appeals Chamber goes to -- or does convict Mr. Simic on aiding and abetting instead of as a member of the JCE, how does that impact on his sentence? Question number 6. Our position is that there is no absolute rule in this Tribunal that an aider and abettor is subject to a lower maximum penalty than a participant in a joint criminal enterprise. We submit that the relevant inquiry for sentencing is the gravity of the crime including a consideration of the nature and degree of the participation of the accused in the crime. If Simic's liability were to be classified -- reclassified solely on the basis of indictment defects, the principal factor in determining sentence remains the gravity of the crime and his role in the crimes. In this case, the Trial Chamber found that Simic had the specific intent to persecute and that his intentions -- or his actions, I'm sorry, furthered the crimes of the co-perpetrators of the joint criminal enterprise. We would submit that the gravity of the offence and his participation are essentially the same as his liability was as that of co-perpetrator of a joint criminal enterprise, because even after the requalification of conviction, Simic would be an aider and abettor with specific intent rather than possessing mere knowledge, and thus little or no reduction would be warranted. The Statute and the Rules do not mandate that aiding and abetting convictions should result in lower sentences than for other forms of liability under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Tribunal jurisprudence confirms that there is no absolute rule. In Vasiljevic, Appeals Chamber decision, the Chamber said, generally, aiders and abettors warrant a lower sentence than participants in a JCE. Generally. The word "generally warrants lower sentences" is also stated in Krstic and comparing it to responsibility as a co-perpetrator. The word "generally" suggests that this Chamber recognises that there is no absolute rule and that the reduction in sentence as a result of recharacterisation of the mode of liability does not automatically result in a reduction in sentence, and that in deciding whether or not a reduction of sentence is warranted as a result of a reclassification, it is our submission that the basic sentencing principles should have more sway in that determination than the simple reclassification itself. And in particular when sentencing, one should pay attention to the fact that where an accused acts with intent, and particularly the intent to persecute, that should have an important factor in either eliminating a reduction or markedly reducing it from previous cases. I point out that in the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgement, it was determined that Krstic lacked genocidal intent, and that resulted in a significant diminishing of his responsibility warranting considerable reduction in his sentence. In Vasiljevic, his sentence was reduced on the basis of being found as an aider and abettor instead of a member of a joint criminal enterprise. And although not stated expressly, it appears that the requirement of shared intent was missing from Vasiljevic's conviction or from the evidence to justify Mr. Vasiljevic's conviction resulting in the reduced sentence. I've already said, and I won't repeat other than for emphasis, that Simic is an aider and abettor with intent. The observation I make in terms of reduction of sentence, if any, that Vasiljevic and Krstic reduced the sentence approximately 25 per cent. They are the only two cases I can point you to specifically on point. I have already mentioned that for Krstic and Vasiljevic, the finding was specifically that they did not -- in Krstic's case he did not have the specific intent. That appears to be the basis upon which Vasiljevic was equally decided, and consequently our position is that any reduction, should the Appeals Chamber consider one on an aiding and abetting conviction, should be smaller than the 25 per cent imposed by the Appeals Chamber as a result of the change of the basis of conviction in Krstic and Vasiljevic. The Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Simic to 17 years' imprisonment. The gravity of the offence and Simic's role in the crimes are the primary factors for determining sentence. The rationale for imposing a 17-year sentence is clear in the Trial Chamber decision. They looked at the relevant factors that Trial Chambers are to consider, the fact that Mr. Simic was the most prominent member of the civilian authority involved in the persecution campaign, the fact that Simic chose to become involved at the highest level of the civilian authorities and assumed an active role, the fact that Simic was found to be acting with specific intent to persecute, and when all of these factors are considered, I would submit on behalf of the Prosecution that if any reduction is warranted, no more than 10 per cent should be considered. With that, I am open for questions, but I have no formal submissions left to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, I am trying to focus on your references to an aider and abettor having the intent. Now, I think I know why you say that. Do correct me if I'm wrong. You take the view that an aider and abettor is guilty of the primary offence and therefore he must have the specific intent to commit that offence, but am I right that under the general law an aider and abettor only has to have knowledge of the principal crime and that he does not have to be proved to be sharing the specific intent to commit that crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We have the same understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have shifted away from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No. I believe that perhaps I was unclear in my submissions. When I was speaking about having the specific intent, I was always referring to Simic -- Dr. Simic having the specific intent. I started my submissions by referring to the Kvocka Appeals Chamber decision which limited the amount of knowledge -- or the amount of intent knowledge, the mens rea to knowledge, and I was never proposing that specific intent was required for the aider and abettor. I was saying that, based on the Trial Chamber's findings in this particular case, Simic was found to have specific intent and that that specific intent didn't change or didn't cease to exist by virtue of the fact that he could be convicted under the alternative mode of liability, being aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would I be correct in understanding you this way: That the accused must be shown to have the specific intent but to aid and abet and not the specific intent to commit the principal crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: He must know that his actions are aiding and abetting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. I have a which might be reserved to your colleague Mr. Wirth. Is he here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I cannot see him. Mr. Wirth, the question has to do with the JCE amendments to the indictment. I understood the Defence to be saying that they objected to those amendments and that the Prosecution was saying no, the Defence did not object to those amendments. Well, I have before me the decision of the Trial Chamber of 20th December, 2001. Now, the Trial Chamber does not use -- the decision of the Trial Chamber does not refer to the word "objection," but it considers very carefully the JCE amendments to the indictment. It grants the amendments in part and refuses the indictment in the other part. Now, doesn't the fact that the Trial Chamber was considering the amendments before deciding whether to grant or refuse them demonstrate that there must have been an objection to those amendments? Maybe the transcript of the proceedings, which I have not consulted, would clarify the position. But meanwhile, the question, to my mind, is this: If the Trial Chamber was deliberating upon the question whether or not to grant these amendments, doesn't the fact that the Trial Chamber was deliberating on that issue suggest that the Defence must have made some objections to the amendments being made?

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to answer the question in two steps. The first step is we are not relying on the fourth amended indictment, which is the indictment that has been amended by the -- that was the result of the 20 December decision. We rely on the third amended indictment, which has been -- leave to file this amendment has been granted in May, 2001, four months before the trial. That is the primary answer. As regards the litigation around the 20 December decision, I can look it up for you, but -- from what I recall from the decision, I think the decision explicitly states that the Defence has not raised any specific questions with regard to inserting the language "acting in concert together." The Defence -- the Trial Chamber says that the Defence set out all amendments to the indictment in their -- in their submission, but then the substance of their argument only went to other issues revolving around the count of destruction of property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, I've listened to you -- I've listened to you, Mr. Wirth. I'm not sure that I have assimilated the decision from a first reading of it in the same way as you understand it, but maybe your colleagues on the opposite side of the court will come to my rescue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a brief question to put to you. I think Mr. Kremer or Ms. Goy can answer that question. During Ms. Goy's submissions with regard to the duty to act and to the ability to act, there was a reference made to the various types of abilities to act, the ability to prevent, the ability to impede, the ability to -- et cetera. Does the ability to act necessarily imply the ability to prevent or the ability to impede? I would like to benefit from the point of view of the Prosecution on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think Ms. Goy is better prepared to deal with that question than I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- we have submitted that in the omission we are dealing with, the omission in terms of a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, it is sufficient to have the ability to impede the furthering of the joint criminal enterprise, to make it more difficult for the other members of the joint criminal enterprise to move ahead rather than to be able to fully prevent the furthering of the common plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But does the ability to act necessarily imply the type of ability you've quoted, ability to impede or ability to prevent?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: We would submit that Simic, in this case, had the required means to impede the furthering of the joint criminal enterprise. It was inherent in his role and authority that he had -- was in a position to influence the other members of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kremer, if I understand correctly, you've finished your submissions. You've completed your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. So if that's the case, we might now give the floor to the Defence for its reply, and the Defence will have until 4.00 p.m. If there is no objection, I'd like to proceed that way, and we'll have a 20-minute break at 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may, I will respond not perhaps in the order in which the Prosecution dealt with the issues but in order to, at the end of my submissions, come back to the two questions which Mr. Wirth addressed, the two outstanding questions from the Appeals Chamber's order of the 5th of May, which I have not yet spoken to. So if I may, Your Honour, let me begin by addressing briefly the submissions made by Ms. Goy, and to some extent Mr. Kremer, dealing with the question of the responsibility of -- of Dr. Simic. First of all, Ms. Goy cited to the Court some authorities that I think were intended to imply that there was some duty under international law which could extend to a civilian commander to protect the civilian population in certain circumstances, almost regardless of an actual ability to do so. I think that must have been the implication of the submissions, because the Trial Chamber found explicitly, as I referenced this morning, that Dr. Simic, in fact, had no authority over the police or the paramilitaries or the military forces of the 17th Tactical Unit. Now, if I'm not mistaken, Your Honour, and I believe that this is correct, there was some reference to it in the briefs, the -- the obligation that Ms. Goy refers to, to protect the civilian population, is an obligation that falls upon the military commander in an area in time of conflict. It's a very specific obligation deriving partly from -- originally from the Geneva Conventions, and we have dealt with that, I think, in outline at pages 66 to 69 of our brief, and I think to some extent also in the reply brief at paragraph 35. Ms. Goy also referenced in support of that the decision in Blaskic at page 663, and Mr. Moore kindly wrote down for me what that paragraph appears to say, and it says -- it says this: "Although criminal responsibility generally requires the commission of a positive act, this is not an absolute requirement as is demonstrated by the responsibility of a commander who fails to finish a subordinate. There is a further exception to the general rule. Perpetration of a crime by omission pur count to Article 7(1), whereby a legal duty is imposed inter alia as a commander to care for the persons under the control of one's subordinates. Wilful failure to discharge such a duty may incur criminal responsibility under 7(1) in the absence of a positive act." That is not, in all due respect, the position of Dr. Simic. The whole question of omission in -- in this context, Your Honour, is, of course, bound up with the Trial Chamber's findings. Both Ms. Goy and Mr. Kremer recited to you a considerable volume of findings from the Trial Chamber's judgement. I am not going to emulate that, but out of fairness to Dr. Simic, I have to briefly put before you the other side of that story. Mr. Kremer used a very telling phrase which I think reveals perhaps some of the misunderstanding that the Prosecution has on this issue. He said that Dr. Simic had installed himself as the president of the Crisis Staff, and the implication seems to be that the Crisis Staff was in some way an illegal organisation. Now, as all of Your Honours know having been involved in cases in this Tribunal, and I think it's abundantly clear we all understand this now, that a Crisis Staff was a unit set up originally in Tito's Yugoslavia as part of the overall defence of the former Yugoslavia, and the way it worked legally was that as soon as there was a declaration of war or the imminent threat of war or a crisis, the normal functioning of government through the municipal assembly ceased, a Crisis Staff came into being, the president of the municipal assembly by operation of law became president of the Crisis Staff for the duration, and that's how it worked. And the fact that Dr. Simic was a politician, even in the former Yugoslavia, Your Honours, is not a criminal act. And the fact that he was the president of the Crisis Staff is not a criminal act. They ask, well -- they actually said in argument this afternoon, well, Dr. Simic could have gone for help to the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska. They made that argument also in -- in their brief, forget apparently that the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, according to the Prosecution's theory of the case, was himself a member of a criminal organisation devoted to the establishment of a Greater Serbia. Was it the Prosecution's intention that Dr. Simic should go to that source for help? We have noted in our brief, Your Honour, at paragraph 60, I'm not going to read these out, the Prosecution has taken enough time doing that, but I would like to refer to the fact that we did present to the Court in our brief a considerable record of findings by the Trial Chamber, this is at paragraph 61, of the work of the Crisis Staff on behalf of all of the population of Samac regardless of ethnic background. The Trial Chamber made some very detailed findings of that, and they found that many of the decisions of the Crisis Staff were not in fact discriminatory. For example, there was a ban on alcohol which applied for the crisis period to all citizens regardless of ethnicity. The ban on political parties was legitimate under international law and applied equally, and so on. There were findings that the Crisis Staff did its guess to distribute basic foodstuffs, medical supplies to the population regardless of ethnicity. So the Prosecution's painting of Dr. Simic and this Crisis Staff as being just one big criminal enterprise is not only unreasonable, it's contrary to the findings of the Trial Chamber, and it's contrary to the known position of the law of the former Yugoslavia as to what a Crisis Staff was and what it was supposed to do. And somehow the Prosecution would have us believe that mere membership of a political body such as a Crisis Staff is a criminal act. Your Honours, it is not. The Trial Chamber did not make a finding that it was. And the task of the courts, if I may say so respectively, is to separate legitimate lawful from unlawful conduct. The Prosecution wants to sweep it all up into one pile and suggests that Dr. Simic should be criminally responsible simply for that. What is the reality here? The reality is that the Crisis Staff was a political body which had no power to control the situation. The Trial Chamber said that time and time again, and despite that, at the Prosecution's urging they said that Dr. Simic, as a person of influence in their view in the municipality should have in some manner controlled these violent offenders who, as Judge Lindholm put it, took advantage of the political situation. We submit simply that the record shows Dr. Simic had no such ability either in law or in fact and was not under a duty under international law to do so. The responsibility for law and order in that time of crisis, according to the very authorities that Ms. Goy cited rested upon the military commander for the area. Now, turning, if I may, to another matter, Mr. Kremer said that I had conceded that aiding and abetting was an appropriate form -- mode of liability, and I hope the Appeals Chamber will recall that I made that concession after first saying that it was my primary contention that the evidence did not support a finding of liability, and I see that Your Honours have that point. Let me return, Your Honours, now to the troubled question of the indictment, which I suspect is really at the heart of our discussion today. I -- I confess to being surprised and troubled at the Prosecution's reaction or perhaps lack of reaction to the circumstances of the third amended indictment. Mr. Wirth told you, and I have -- I accept completely what he says, that yesterday the Prosecution consulted the Registry and were told that the version of the indictment on the record was the one including the language "acting in concert" and "common purpose." I accept that completely. But it raises more questions than it answers. We filed our reply brief in 2004 and at that point we raised this problem. The Prosecution was aware of what we were saying because shortly after we filed the reply brief we got a motion to strike that part of it which the Appeals Chamber denied. And one has to ask why is it that the Prosecution yesterday is going to the registry to try to get an answer for this when they knew that this issue was there right from August of 2004? And the issue, let me be quite clear, is this: I accept that what is on the record is the version of the indictment that has been referred to containing the language the Prosecution relies upon, but how is it possible that a second version of that indictment has found its way into circulation, including to the public website of this Tribunal, and how is it possible that the Pre-Trial Chamber signed off on an indictment that contained additional language when it had been explicitly represented to them by the Prosecution that the only purpose of the amendment was to delete certain charges and to remove Article 7(3) responsibility for Dr. Simic? And I had hoped when this was raised this morning to be as perhaps as Your Honours expected, to be given an explanation of this that would at least help us towards resolving that troubling question, because on the face of it -- I'm trying now to speak with moderation. On the face of it, unless otherwise explained, it seems that somebody deceived the Pre-Trial Chamber into signing off on an indictment that they did not believe they were signing. And for the Prosecution now to say, "Well, we abandoned the fourth amended indictment because language is there in the third amended indictment," asking the Appeals Chamber to turn its back on this problem and say, "Well, we really ignore the fact that this happened, and despite that we will assume that the Defence were given notice and that everything was proper," is little short of outrageous. Your Honour, the -- when one considers the history of this case and other cases, with everything that the Appeals Chamber has said time and time and time again about the necessity for detailed pleading -- in Kvocka the Appeals Chamber said that the indictment must be pleaded with sufficient detail. If it is defective, the Appeals Chamber may reverse the conviction. In the same case, the Appeals Chamber added that JCE responsibility must be specifically pleaded. And time and time again we've set these quotations out more than once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just remind you that still have only ten minutes before the break. Of course, you can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I appreciate it. In the Krnojelac case, we see again that the Appeals Chamber is saying specifically that the pleading must be precise. In Blaskic you come back to that same theme. And perhaps this will be a good way, Your Honour, just before the break, and then I will come back and answer the two specific questions for you, but perhaps let me just say this leading up to the break as a general observation, that it is my submission in this case that not only was the state of the pleading obviously defective, not only did it cause unfairness to Dr. Simic, but that in addition to that our submission is that the time has come when the Appeals Chamber should say in effect enough is enough. We make rules for -- to be obeyed. These are important practical rules, and the Prosecution's reaction to our appeal on this issue has simply one of casual disregard. In their response brief they say, "Well, the pleadings were perfectly proper," even though even the Trial Chamber said they were very far from proper. And now, confronted with the fact that the very indictment that they seek to rely upon is shrouded in this unsavory motion to seek to amend, they nevertheless say, We rely on that and that is our position. Now, Your Honour, there -- the other issue that has been raised is whether "acting in concert" and "common purpose" is sufficient language. Mr. Wirth described that as the classical language of a joint criminal enterprise. As I indicated before lunch in response to questions from the Bench, we do not suggest that the words "joint criminal enterprise" necessarily have to appear as such in every indictment, but what does have to appear in every indictment is the substance -- the substantive pleading of both the facts and the allegations on which the Prosecution relies, and they must correspond to the basic elements of a joint criminal enterprise in whatever language that is couched. And it's common ground in this appeal, Your Honours, common ground, that that could not have happened before the third amended indictment, and we would submit that even the addition of that language in the circumstances, when taken with the pre-trial brief, which is clearly directed towards an aiding and abetting theory, is not sufficient notice to put Dr. Simic fairly on notice that he is in a trial for a joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, I'm now coming really to answer the last two questions. Would it be convenient to take a break a few minutes early and then I can finish very rapidly, I think, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] Your Honours raised two questions, the second and third question in the order of the 5th of May, which I would submit essentially raised the question of whether the procedure taken in the whole of this case was fair to Dr. Simic, and in light of my earlier submissions in response to the first question, I, of course, put before the Appeals Chamber then the proposition that in general, even if an indictment is defective it would be open to the Prosecution to cure it by means of the pre-trial brief. But in any event, I would submit in light of the Appeals Chamber's principles laid down in the Krnojelac case the position should be clarified by the beginning of the trial. And so essentially we have to resolve this case, I submit, by looking at what the situation was at the beginning of trial. Had the Prosecution done enough at that point to fairly put Dr. Simic on notice of the case that he had to meet. Now, what we have here, taking it at its best from the Prosecution's point of view, is a pre-trial brief that does not address the question of joint criminal enterprise combined, at best, with an amended indictment which in one place states "acting in concert together" and in one place uses the phrase "common purpose", but in all other respects pleads facts that are really more consistent with the position taken in the pre-trial brief, and that really is the state of play as this trial begins. Three months into the trial -- and let me add in parenthesis as the Trial Chamber noted, that position was not corrected at the pre-trial conference or in the opening statement of the Prosecution. Three months into trial, as the Appeals Chamber observes in its second question, we have the issue of what the Trial Chamber called harmonising or cleaning up the language of the existing indictment, and what that amounted to essentially was to take the same language and instead of stating it once to add it to a number to other paragraphs in the amended indictment. And that was the final state of the pleadings as was mentioned by my colleague Mr. Pantelic. The other amendment was simply a technical amendment to remove the accused Milan Simic from the proceedings. And that remained the state of play until the 92 bis motion that the Prosecution at last revealed their true colours and said there was a joint criminal enterprise of which Dr. Simic was a part. And it is our submission in response to questions 2 and 3 that even assuming in the Prosecution's favour that that language was used in the third amended indictment, and those now become critical because the Prosecution abandoned reliance on the fourth amended indictment, they've nailed their colours firmly to the mass here. So if the Appeals Chamber thinks that the third amendment indictment was not sufficient, then that really does decide the issue of fairness in favour of Dr. Simic. And what the Appeals Chamber has to decide, I would submit, is whether looking at that history as a whole it can say that Dr. Simic was given a fair trial, that he was put appropriately on notice. And it's our submission, very simply, that he was not. Now, I'm going to come back at the very end of my submission, which I assure the Court will not be long delayed, to the -- to some matters that I think flow from that, the answers to those questions, but let me at this point, before I do, come briefly to the issue of sentence. Mr. Kremer responded also to the question that Your Honours had posed about what effect would be produced on the sentence if we were to reclassify the mode of responsibility in some manner in favour of Dr. Simic, and we had some numerical discussions that I frankly did not follow very well, it seemed to be more related to the stock exchange, 10 per cent reduction, 25 per cent reduction. Your Honours, let me suggest that with all due respect the right way to decide this is not in those terms but by looking at what the situation is overall and bearing in mind this is the first kind of its kind in the sense that it's the first case in the history of the Tribunal where we've had a dissenting opinion on the issue of sentence and a very dramatic difference, really, between 7 and 17 years. Judge Lindholm, a very experienced Judge, took have a very different view of that sentencing, and we've therefore been provided with a benchmark here so we don't simply have to cast about for individual opinions, certainly not from the bar. We've had a judicial opinion on this subject which we submit carries great weight. But the whole issue of sentence should be looked at, I submit, in that manner and dealt with really in response to the findings that the Trial Chamber makes about the appropriate responsibility. We would submit that Judge Lindholm's opinion in that regard is entitled to -- to great weight. We would submit, in fact, that it should be used as a starting point. And I also remind the Chamber, respectfully, that there's also one other very usual aspect of this case flowing from the Prosecution's failure to identify the true nature of the case, and that is that we had two co-accused who we now know, according to the Prosecution, were also involved in the joint criminal enterprise. We didn't know that at the time, but during the trial they changed their pleas. They pleaded guilty, and as the record will reflect were sentenced on the basis of the Court thought the appropriate -- what the state of the case was at that time. And it seems anomalous, to say the least, and certainly almost random that because Dr. Simic maintained his plea of not guilty and the goal posts, if I can using a sporting analogy, were moved on him during the trial and he ended up being the apex of a joint criminal enterprise and sentenced to this really in an extraordinary way to 17 years. And the Appeals Chamber may think, I submit, that fairness here almost demands that Dr. Simic's sentence be reconciled in the sense of being much more approximated to that of the other participants in -- in this case, that it would be anomalous to leave this much higher sentence out there when there was such a confusion caused by the Prosecution itself in identifying the true nature of the case. I have one final submission, Your Honour, and then I will of course answer willingly any questions you have. And this is much more a general submission. It's not raised specifically by any of questions, although it does impact -- it does flow from some of the questions the Court has asked today. We invite the Appeals Chamber to say that this case should not be only about finding a just result in Dr. Simic's appeal but should also be used as an opportunity to lay down principles partly along the lines that Your Honour, really indicated in -- in the questions that you posed to us bearing in mind the -- what we submit to be the casual attitude of the Prosecution towards -- not only towards pleading but towards the third amended indictment. I'm going to ask the Court to bear with me on this for one or two minutes. Certain questions have been raised about whether or not the Defence at the time of trial made appropriate objections to the indictment, to the amended to the indictment, to the fact that they were taken by surprise. These questions have not perhaps been satisfactorily resolved in all respects today. Nevertheless, there are certain cases -- the Prosecution likes to regard waiver as a sort of absolute rule. It is not. It is not. Sometimes there are more fundamental issues that arise in a case, and I'm going to ask the Appeals Chamber to say that even if, and let me assume now for the sake of argument only that we agree with everything the Prosecution says on that subject, let us say that no notice or objection was made by the Defence, we would respectfully submit in this case and having regard to the implications in this case, the Prosecution's conduct overall has been so egregious that given the lack of objection that should be overridden by the need to ensure fairness. If the Court feels that the history of this matter reveals a defective pleading that was unfair to Dr. Simic, there are really three things that the Appeals Chamber could do to redress that. One of them Your Honours have asked us to address today, but I would like for the sake of completeness to address all three. I'm going to call them, if I may use this shorthand, the logical remedy, the remedy slightly less favourable to Dr. Simic, and a remedy slightly more favourable to Dr. Simic. The logical remedy is top grant Dr. Simic a new trial on the basis of full notice and information. Let me say immediately, having regard to the completion strategy of the Tribunal as well as to probably the potential of bringing back the witnesses I realise that is not a reasonable case. That leaves us therefore with two choices, perhaps not favourable to Mr. Simic the one that Your Honours have averted to, to make an adjustment in the sentence accordingly and if that is the view that the Appeals Chamber takes then of course the Defence appreciates that, but I am bold enough to make this submission in the particular circumstances of this case, that there is also another remedy somewhat more favourable to Dr. Simic, and I invite the Appeals Chamber to apply it, and that is that -- to recognise that unless the Prosecution is faced with consequences, tangible consequences for their attitude toward the rules this way of pleading is never going to change and Your Honours are going to be dealing with this way ever pleading until the day the Tribunal closes its doors because as long as they get away with this kind of practice and despite the clear criticism of the Trial Chamber can say to this Appeals Chamber our pleadings are in complete order, they maintain that position today, until there are tangible sanctions against that, it's never going to change. What I invite you to do respectfully Your Honours is to say the proper course of action here is to substitute a verdict of acquittal on behalf of Dr. Simic and bring this to an end. And with that I am ready to answer any questions that Your Honours may have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This hearing has been complicated by references to a number of amendments of a number of indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I have in mind the third amended indictment, and there is, I believe, an impression that there were two versions of that indictment involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One on the web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And one, shall I say, on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, can you assist me by saying which of the two did the Defence receive?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, maybe Mr. Pantelic could address that because he was there at trial, and rather than repeat what he's told me, I think it might be best to ask him to address you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can confirm that we received third amended indictment on 24th of April, 2001, with the Prosecutor motion for leave to amend, which was cited by my learned friend, Professor Murphy, where the -- the -- it was actually explanations with regard to Dr. Simic that mode of liability 7(3) has been deleted. And it's just technical -- technical issue. Your Honour, if I may add with regard to the other inquiry that you made before, Trial Chamber issued its decision on December 20, 2001, regarding the motion for leave to amend the indictment, actually amended the third indictment. So we are speaking about the fourth amended indictment. You have this decision, and you posed a question to my learned friend from the Prosecution. Well, in the overall atmosphere that we were facing during trial, the best explanation was -- can we find in paragraph 29 of this decision. The Trial Chamber said: "In conclusion, in issuing this decision on the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend the third amended indictment, the Trial Chamber finds that many of the issues raised are due to the lack of diligence on the part of the Prosecution." And it was repeated in Trial Chamber again. And it was also stated in paragraph 25 of the said decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 25, yes. Where you can see at the bottom of this paragraph on page 7: 'The Trial Chamber will only permit the inclusion of this paragraph in relation to persecution." There were certain discussions about the words "acting in concert together". As usual, the Prosecution tried to include all these formulations for all charges, you know, on the back door. It was a permanent practice during trial. And the reaction of the Trial Chamber was, "No. You should stop with this practice. We will give you -- we will allow you only to include this particular wording on paragraph -- paragraph 40." And in addition -- well, kind of -- I consider it a kind of balance. In addition to that, in paragraph 20 the Trial Chamber stated that it was some kind of cleaning up the inconsistencies of language, et cetera, et cetera. So, Your Honour, in sum, the position of Defence is the following: In accordance with the -- all elements of the Prosecution theory, we as a Defence proceeded with our defence strategy in terms of 7(1) liability with various forms with a focus to aiding and abetting, and that was our strategy. We did not object formally to this kind of language forms simply because it was our understanding of -- it was our knowledge of that case. Obviously, Prosecution shifted in its understanding of the case from 1995, 1995, up to 2002, and we explained all this development. The issue here is, I stress again, whether Dr. Simic was an active participant in joint criminal enterprise or he was an aider and abettor. That's our point. I believe it to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I was only on the question of the identity of the indictment which you received. You say it's the indictment referred to in paragraph 20 of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Are there any other questions, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there aren't any other questions from my colleagues, we've come to the end of the submissions of the parties in this hearing. You can sit down, Mr. Murphy. I'm now going to turn to Mr. Simic, and I shall ask him if he wants to take the floor for a brief statement to the Appeals Chamber according to what was stated in the Scheduling Order. You have the floor, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any interpretation from B/C/S into English? Wait a minute, please. Can the technicians help us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you now, yes. I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have our technical problems been solved now? Can you hear me? You have the floor, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will repeat what I have said. I have nothing to add in connection with my defence, because everything I wanted to say has already been said by my counsel. I would, however, like to take this opportunity to thank you for enabling me to visit the graves of my deceased parents on two occasions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down. So this is now the end of this appeals hearing in this case. Before adjourning, I would like to address one last point. According to Rule 65 bis, a status conference is to be organised before mid-June 2006 so that Mr. Simic can raise any questions dealing with his conditions of detention or dealing with his state, his mental and physical state, health. So as the Pre-Trial Judge, I would like know, Mr. Simic, whether you have any questions to raise regarding this. You don't. Thank you. Therefore, it won't be necessary to organise a status conference before the next 120 days. Does the Prosecution have any objection to raise regarding this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on behalf of this Appeals Chamber, I now would like to thank the counsels for Defence and representatives of the Prosecution for their collaboration, as well as legal officers and Registry officers have I with helped us for this hearing. I would also like to thank the court reporters for their great help, very precious help, and also the interpreters, who make it possible, who helped us behind the stage to make this hearing possible. Now we may adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: at 4.51 p.m.
